88e050b78d1d42a4: KOTA BHARU, Oct 31 — The Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) did not interfere in the decision to return former Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain to the Royal Malaysian Police (PDRM).
Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said his office was only responsible for providing legal advice but the issue regarding Mohd Shuhaily was an administrative matter for the ministry.
“We have not given an official opinion because it has not been referred to AGC, it is just an administrative action by KDN (Home Ministry), so we will not interfere in that.

“Whether Datuk Mohd Shuhaily wants to stay there or be transferred back to the PDRM, we will not interfere... that is more of an administrative matter,” he told reporters after the Opening Ceremony of the Handover of the Kampung Angkat MADANI (KAM) AGC 2026 Recreational Infrastructure at Taman Pinggiran Warisan, Kampung Kok Lanas here today.
On Thursday, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said Mohd Shuhaily returned to duty with the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) after a decision was made last week.
Earlier, former policeman, Saifuddin Abdul Kader, requested the Attorney General’s intervention so that the investigation into his beating by Mohd Shuhaily in 2015, could be reopened.

Lawyers representing Saifuddin, Kamal Hisham Ja’afar and Muhammad Nor Tamrin reportedly said that their client lodged a police report against Mohd Shuhaily on November 19, 2015 when he was serving as the Hilir Perak district police chief.

Meanwhile, in the development regarding the separation of the roles of the Public Prosecutor and the Attorney General, Mohd Dusuki said that his party is drafting a provision regarding the method of selecting the candidate.

Previously, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Law and Institutional Reform), Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said gave the Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) two weeks to provide detailed feedback on the proposal to separate the roles of the Public Prosecutor and the Attorney General.
He said that the Parliamentary Special Select Committee (PSSC) would meet again after receiving views on the matter. — Bernama
145238846887b4a5: KUALA LUMPUR: Former Dutch striker Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink came within 13 goals of reaching a century for Chelsea, but when asked which defenders made life difficult for him during his playing days, he had two names ready.
Arsenal's Sol Campbell and Manchester United's Rio Ferdinand.
Hasselbaink scored 87 goals in 136 appearances for Chelsea between 2000 and 2004, establishing himself as one of the Premier League's most feared forwards.
Although he won the Golden Boot twice during his career, he never reached the 100-goal mark at Stamford Bridge.
Asked which defenders had made life difficult for him, Hasselbaink singled out Campbell and Ferdinand, revealing that the latter was a troublesome opponent.

"I didn't like playing against Campbell. I didn't like playing against Ferdinand. Only once I scored against Ferdinand. Only once. But I found it very, very difficult. He was very good. Very good," he said.
For a striker known for his goalscoring prowess, Ferdinand clearly stood out as a defender who could make him work for every opportunity.
But Hasselbaink believes the demands on strikers have changed considerably since his time in English football, with modern forwards receiving greater protection from referees.
Asked whether he would have found it easier to score against today's defenders, the former Netherlands international was confident he would have benefited from the changes.

"Now, scoring the goals, for sure, for sure. Because back in the day, in my games, it was a lot tougher. It was a lot harder. They could tackle harder. The strikers are getting protected so much more, so much more. So, you have to just use your brain a little bit more," he said.
Hasselbaink, however, was reluctant to suggest that modern players had become softer, pointing instead to the way referees now officiate physical challenges.
He cited Morgan Rogers' tackle on Everton midfielder James Garner as an example of a hard but fair challenge, arguing that such tackles were once a normal part of defending.

The introduction of video assistant refereeing (VAR) has also changed the scrutiny surrounding challenges, prompting Hasselbaink to acknowledge that the technology might not always have worked in his favour.
"I wouldn't say softer. I wouldn't use the word soft because I don't think that the players are soft. I just think that the referee blows a little bit quicker," he said.
"If that was VAR, I would be in trouble," he added.

Hasselbaink also offered his assessment of two Ballon d'Or winners from different generations, Michael Owen and Harry Kane, having played against Owen and later coached Kane during his time with England.

He remembered Owen as a quick, direct forward whose game was affected by hamstring injuries, while praising Kane's all-round attacking qualities and ability to create opportunities for his team-mates.

"In that time, Owen was very quick, very direct. But when he got injured on his hamstrings, he lost a lot," said Hasselbaink, who was an assistant to Gareth Southgate with the England national team from 2023 to 2024.
"Kane is somebody who can score all kinds of goals, all kinds of assists he can give. And technically, he is such a good player."
Asked whom he would prefer to have in his team, Hasselbaink chose Kane, pointing to what the England captain has achieved over the years.
"So, if I have to choose, I would choose Harry Kane. What he has done over the years, you have to clap your hands for him and you have to say, well done," he added.
For the record, Owen won the Premier League Golden Boot in the 1997-98 and 1998-99 seasons after scoring 18 goals in each campaign.
Kane has enjoyed even greater success in front of goal, winning three Premier League Golden Boots (2015-16, 2016-17 and 2020-21).
He was also the top scorer with six goals at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

Kane further underlined his prolific reputation by winning the Bundesliga's Golden Boot in his debut season with Bayern Munich in 2023-24, scoring 36 league goals, and successfully defending the award in 2024-25 with 26 goals.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

a22bc6bee8dfde64: JASIN: Barisan Nasional candidate for the Merlimau seat Datuk Dr Muhamad Akmal Saleh is banking on his five-year service record to regain voters' confidence in the Melaka state election.
He said residents, particularly those in Merlimau, could assess his performance and contributions during his term before making their decision on polling day.
"People in Merlimau know what I have done. That is why I have no problem responding to all the criticism because I am offering my service.

"If they feel my service has not been good, I honestly say they should not vote for me. But if they feel my service has been good and satisfactory, I ask for their trust once again," he said after the nomination process at Dewan Platinum, Politeknik Merlimau.
Dr Akmal, who is also Umno Youth chief, will face a straight fight against Pakatan Harapan (PH) candidate and state Amanah Wanita chief Rahayu Hamzah.
The incumbent Merlimau assemblyman remained optimistic despite facing various challenges and criticism throughout his political career.
He said challenges were part and parcel of politics for any leader, and such experiences should be seen as opportunities for self-improvement.
He cited several national leaders who had remained in politics despite facing various controversies and criticism.

"(Prime Minister) Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has faced all kinds of criticism, yet he remains prime minister to this day. The same goes for (Deputy Prime Minister) Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who has also faced various issues.
"As a leader, I believe these are part and parcel of what we have to go through. God willing, these challenges will make me a better person in the future," he said.
Dr Akmal said he had therefore chosen to let his service record speak for itself, while hoping voters would give him another opportunity to continue serving the constituency.

He expressed confidence that his experience over the past five years would help him face the challenges of this election, adding that the people's support and trust would determine whether he received another mandate.
ca8827ca4a1d6f84: PETALING JAYA: Melaka DAP chief Khoo Poay Tiong claims Barisan Nasional will appoint PAS representatives as appointed assemblymen should the BN-Perikatan Nasional alliance win the Nov 14 state election.
Khoo, the Kota Melaka MP, believed that PAS would not be satisfied with only being allocated two seats in the Melaka polls, even if the Islamic party wins both seats.
He claimed that state BN chief Ab Rauf Yusoh was using the appointed assemblyman positions to cut deals, even with MCA after its protest over initial seat allocations, Sin Chew reported.
"He is simply using the seven appointed assemblyman positions as bargaining chips for BN. When MCA protested, he used these positions to appease them,” Khoo was quoted as saying.
He claimed Rauf had already promised MCA two of the seven appointed assemblyman posts.
Pakatan Harapan withdrew from the BN-led Melaka government in July following the passage of a constitutional amendment to allow the appointment of up to seven unelected state assemblymen.
PH contended that the amendment was at odds with democratic principles, although Sabah, Terengganu and Pahang also allow this.
Rauf had defended the move, saying the posts would be allocated to experts and professionals.
BN is contesting 23 seats in the Melaka polls under an alliance with PN, which is vying for the remaining five.

55cc45ce3f1aadc2: WASHINGTON, Oct 31 — A US federal judge temporarily blocked on Friday the Justice Department from threatening state and local election officials with criminal prosecution if they fail to comply with its directives on processing ballots.

The order by Judge Trina Thompson in the Northern District of California deals a setback to Trump administration efforts to restrict voting by people it says might not be US citizens in the November 3 midterm elections.
The harshly worded temporary restraining order was issued in response to a case brought by labour union and civil rights groups against the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security.

“Defendants shall not threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots of any registered voter solely on the basis that the ballot belongs to an individual alleged by Defendants to be ineligible to vote,” Thompson wrote.
The judge also ruled that Justice Department officials “shall not threaten state or local election officials and workers with criminal prosecution for failure to comply” with such demands.

President Donald Trump’s Republican Party is at risk of losing its control of Congress in next Tuesday’s elections, and critics have accused his administration of trying to cast doubt on electoral results.

On Wednesday, a federal judge rejected the Justice Department’s efforts to set aside the ballots of more than 20,000 California voters it said might not be citizens, slamming the move as brazen pre-election “interference.”

In Friday’s ruling, Thompson said that a restraining order, which expires on November 16, was justified “given the fast-approaching date of the Election” and because the plaintiffs “have demonstrated that they will likely succeed on the merits of their claims.”
Thompson described the “intimidation” and threats of criminal prosecution of election workers as “contrary to law” and “arbitrary and capricious.”

In a wide-ranging order, the judge said the defendants shall not demand the removal of specific registered voters from voter lists, nor refuse to issue ballots to specific voters nor demand ballots not be counted because of alleged ineligibility to vote.
For months, Trump – who has never acknowledged his own election defeat by Joe Biden in 2020 – has been claiming that there will be fraud in this year’s midterms.
Studies repeatedly show that while rare cases of voter fraud exist, such incidents are minuscule and do not influence US election results. — AFP

def78158e0c1bfa9: KUALA LUMPUR: National hockey coach Brendan Carolan wants the Speedy Tigers to bridge the gap with the world's elite sides as they prepare to face defending champions India in the Asian Champions Trophy tomorrow.
Malaysia take on the hosts at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Jalandhar, Punjab, on the back of rising to world No. 12 following pool wins over South Korea (3-1) and Bangladesh (6-1).
"We don't just look to finish top two, but we want to close the gap on the big teams ahead of us," Carolan said.

"We will take it game by game and focus on India first before we think of the Japan match. India are a good team, but we need to play better against them. It is a challenge, but we will show them what we can do in the match."
The Speedy Tigers are now the second highest-ranked side in Asia behind world No. 8 India.
Both teams have nine points from three matches, though the hosts lead the table on goal difference.
Six teams are competing in the tournament, with the top four advancing to the semi-finals after the single round-robin stage.
Malaysia conclude their pool fixtures against world No. 16 Japan on Monday.
India, chasing a sixth title, enter the contest in formidable form after wins over Bangladesh (13-0), China (5-2), and Japan (4-1).

Captain Harmanpreet Singh poses a threat after scoring five penalty corner goals in three matches, backed by a dangerous forward line featuring Abhishek, Sukhjeet Singh, Dilpreet Singh, Mandeep Singh, and Shilanand Lakra.
Malaysia face an uphill task, having not defeated India since the semi-finals of the 2018 Jakarta-Palembang Asian Games.
In their most recent encounter, India won 5-1 in the final of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games to secure qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Friday's results: Malaysia 6 Bangladesh 1, South Korea 2 China 1, India 4 Japan 1.
Tomorrow's fixtures: South Korea v Bangladesh (5pm), China v Japan (7.15pm), Malaysia v India (9.30pm)

40a4b3d9f4eb707b: MELAKA, Oct 31 — Barisan Nasional (BN) will continue to entrust Datuk Seri Dr Ab Rauf Yusoh with the post of Chief Minister if the coalition wins the 16th Melaka state election on Nov 14.

BN chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said, however, that the proposal to allow Ab Rauf to continue serving as Chief Minister was subject to the powers vested in Melaka Yang Dipertua Negeri Tun Dr Mohd Ali Mohd Rustam.
“We will not pre-empt the powers vested in the Melaka Yang Dipertua Negeri, but as BN chairman, I will propose Ab Rauf’s name for him to continue serving in Melaka.

“However, we will first return this mandate to the people of Melaka. I hope their support will be translated into votes, enabling us to form the state government together with our strategic partners,” he said.

He told reporters this after accompanying Ab Rauf to the nomination centre for the Tanjung Bidara state constituency at Dewan Datuk Kapt (B) Hj Ab Karim, JAPERUN Tanjung Bidara Complex in Alor Gajah here today.
Ahmad Zahid also expressed hope that the people of Melaka would carefully assess the performance of the state government under Ab Rauf’s leadership before making their decision on polling day.
“We also do not want smear campaigns or campaigns being undermined by various improper tactics, and I expect the campaign atmosphere in Melaka to be relatively calm,” he said.
He also confirmed that BN, together with its strategic partner Perikatan Nasional (PN), would contest all 28 state seats in the Melaka election, describing this as a manifestation of togetherness.
“UMNO is contesting 18 seats, MCA four seats and MIC one seat, while the remaining seats are contested by our partners in PN.

“This demonstrates togetherness, at a time when many had expected MCA to boycott the Melaka state election or, at the very least, to be unhappy with the arrangement. However, this did not happen. Instead, MCA was allocated four seats,” he said.
The Election Commission (EC) has set Nov 14 as polling day for the 16th Melaka state election, while early voting will be held on Nov 10.
For the latest news on the 16th Melaka state election, visit https://election.bernama.com/prn/melaka/2026/. — Bernama
451f5b0666b5b6ab: MELAKA, Oct 31 — Barisan Nasional (BN) supports the signing of a Confidence and Supply Agreement (CSA) between the government, Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu), and several independent Members of Parliament, and has proposed extending the agreement to other parties from both the government and Opposition blocs.
BN Chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the agreement was a positive development, particularly in addressing the needs and concerns of the people.
“This is a positive development, particularly in terms of addressing the needs and concerns of the people.

“Such a constructive approach was also adopted by the government during the tenure of an Umno representative as Prime Minister,” said the Deputy Prime Minister when asked about the CSA, which was signed last Thursday.

Earlier today, Ahmad Zahid accompanied Melaka Chief Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ab Rauf Yusoh to the nomination centre for the Tanjung Bidara constituency at the Datuk Kapt (B) Hj Ab Karim Hall in the Tanjung Bidara Development and Coordination Committee (Japerun) complex in Alor Gajah.

On Thursday, the Madani government signed a CSA with six Bersatu Members of Parliament, led by the party’s president, Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin, and seven other MPs, including Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim was reported to have said that the agreement was intended to ensure continuity of government administration, while providing the necessary space to implement the national development agenda effectively, including the 2027 Budget, for the benefit of the people. — Bernama
1110f9ae088d7b4b: SEPANG, Oct 31 — Jorge Martin’s world championship hopes took a big hit today when he was ruled out of the Malaysian MotoGP sprint and main race with a broken wrist.
The Spaniard arrived in Kuala Lumpur with a fracture from last weekend’s Australian Grand Prix sprint race.
The Aprilia rider came through unscathed in yesterday’s first practice session at Sepang but then only managed a limited number of laps in the afternoon and on today morning.

He did not come out for qualifying and said of the impact on his title hopes: “For for sure I will fight till the end, not only for me, because at the end of the day I’m already a champion, but for my team, for my people, I will fight till the end.”
The 2024 champion’s premature exit is a huge boost to current leader and reigning champion Marc Marquez of Ducati.
Marquez leads his fellow Spaniard Martin by 10 points in the championship with three race weekends left after this.
Martin is now in a race to be ready to compete in Qatar next weekend.
“We’ve decided to withdraw (him) from the rest of the weekend,” said Aprilia Racing team manager Paolo Bonora.
“He couldn’t put any force into the bike in the braking areas.
“He’ll return to Spain and assess the Qatar GP in the coming days.” — AFP
b54f2146f0fb7d9d: PETALING JAYA: A total of 79 candidates will contest the 16th Melaka state election, the Election Commission (EC) announced.

This is a less crowded field compared with the 2021 state polls, when 112 candidates vied for the 28 seats up for grabs as Barisan Nasional, Pakatan Harapan and Perikatan Nasional clashed in all constituencies.
In a statement, EC chairman Ramlan Harun said PH is fielding the most candidates at 24, followed by BN (23), Bersama (16), Bersatu (7), PN (5) and Putra (1)
Three independent candidates are also contesting in the polls.
The 79 candidates comprise 65 men and 14 women.
The state election will see 11 straight fights, 11 three-cornered contests, and six four-cornered battles.
The four-cornered contests will take place in Gadek, Kelebang, Pengkalan Batu, Ayer Keroh, Bukit Katil and Bemban.
The oldest candidate is PH’s Mohamad Jaafar in Telok Mas, aged 66, while the youngest candidate is PH’s 24-year-old candidate, Mukhlisul Mubin Julasapiyah, in Kuala Linggi.
A total of 687,697 voters are eligible to cast their ballots in Melaka. The EC has set Nov 14 as polling day, with early voting taking place on Nov 10.

6f2278fea9c4ba0b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 31 — A primarily US-owned startup is planning a US$600 million (RM2.4 billion) investment in a Malaysian rare-earth refinery, aiming to develop a new critical minerals supply chain as Washington moves to reduce its reliance on China.

DTEC Mineral and Metal Technology expects to establish the facility within three years, chief executive officer Milan Perlly said in an interview. The startup recently became the first company to receive permission under Malaysia’s relaxed export regulations to ship unprocessed rare-earth material to the US, Bloomberg reported.
“The larger goal is to make Malaysia the rare-earth elements processing hub for ionic clay in the region,” Perlly said.

Much of Malaysia’s identified rare-earth wealth lies in ion-adsorption clay deposits. These elements bind loosely to clay rather than locking into hard rock, making extraction cheaper and more efficient. Crucially, they contain the heavy rare earths vital for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and advanced military technology.
DTEC Mineral plans an initial processing capacity of 5,000 tonnes annually. The company ultimately envisions two facilities in Malaysia with a combined output of 10,000 tonnes a year.
“The US wants us to build 10,000 metric tons output,” he said. “My goal is to put one plant on the east coast for 5,000 metric tons, a second plant on the west coast.”

Perlly noted the firm is evaluating sites after holding discussions with state officials in Kedah, Terengganu, Perak, and Negeri Sembilan. These new facilities would expand Malaysia’s rare-earth footprint beyond the existing Pahang operations run by Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths Ltd.

Moving forward, DTEC Mineral intends to develop locally sourced ionic-clay deposits and eventually operate its own mine. While government data places Malaysia's rare-earth resources at an estimated 16.1 million tonnes, much of this remains commercially unproven.
To determine the most suitable processing technology, the company is preparing to ship 30 tonnes of unprocessed material to the US for research, having secured approval to export up to 700 tonnes.

Perlly, a Malaysian-born US citizen and former Capital One executive, holds a 51 per cent stake in DTEC Mineral alongside business partner David Greer. Local firm DTEC Engineering and Construction owns the remaining 49 per cent.
The startup harbours ambitions for a dual listing on Bursa Malaysia and either the Nasdaq or New York Stock Exchange.
DTEC was part of a critical minerals pact signed between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last year.

According to the company's website, the agreement makes DTEC eligible for funding from the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the US International Development Finance Corporation, and the Department of Defense.
21075dc8fe0f1a99: SINGAPORE, Oct 31 — Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has warned business founders that staying at the helm for too long can leave younger leaders underdeveloped and companies less prepared for the future, urging firms to plan leadership succession deliberately.
The Straits Times reported that Wong made the remarks at the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s (SCCCI) 120th anniversary dinner last night.

He reportedly said succession was among the hardest challenges for businesses, particularly family-owned firms, because founders often spend decades building companies around their judgment, relationships and personal identity.
“Renewal cannot be left to chance. It must be planned for, and nurtured deliberately,” he was quoted as saying.

Wong said senior leaders should mentor successors, share their experience and networks, and gradually give younger leaders more responsibility, including room to make their own decisions and mistakes.
Younger leaders, meanwhile, should earn that trust by bringing fresh ideas and capabilities while remaining willing to learn from those who built the business, he said.

Wong said the same principle applied to institutions such as SCCCI, which could connect generations of business leaders, facilitate mentorship and create opportunities for younger members to step forward.
Beyond succession, he urged companies to transform before circumstances forced them to, noting that artificial intelligence was already changing how firms operate and compete.

He cautioned that simply adopting AI tools would not amount to meaningful transformation, saying companies would gain more by rethinking processes, redesigning jobs and, where necessary, changing business models.
172b19a46f5f0435: PETALING JAYA: National badminton legend Lee Chong Wei says that serving as chairman of the Badminton Association of Malaysia's (BAM) performance committee has not been an easy responsibility, especially in making decisions involving players from a different generation.
Chong Wei, who was appointed to the position on Oct 18 last year, said the difference between current players and those of his generation made it difficult to bring about changes, Bernama reported.
Instead, he said, it required him to continue learning and adapting to the challenges he faced.

1fb4bfe9bce21a7a: BEIJING: China's factory activity slipped back into contraction territory in October, official data showed Saturday, despite sustained growth in high-tech industries, as the market for consumer goods weakened.
The manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI), a closely watched gauge of industrial health, came in at 49.3 this month, below the 50 mark separating expansion from contraction.

The fall in manufacturing activity was in part driven by a week-long national holiday at the start of the month, as well as a "complex and volatile international environment", according to NBS statistician Huo Lihui.
The figure, from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), missed the forecast of 49.9 by a Bloomberg survey of economists and was below the 50.1 and 49.8 recorded in September and August respectively
However, it was above the 49.2 recorded in July.
Prices for international crude oil have continued to climb, hiking up the prices of coal, rubber and plastic products, Huo said.

Despite "positive development momentum" within the high-tech sector fuelling the artificial intelligence boom, the PMI for the consumer goods industry in October was down 1.9 percentage points from the previous month, showing that "market activity has somewhat weakened", he added.
Beijing is hoping for annual growth this year of 4.5 to 5.0 percent, its lowest goal in decades, as sluggish domestic demand weighs on its export strength.
"Strong exports alone are not enough to boost the economic momentum," said Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.
"If the external demand weakens in 2027, China will need more significant policy support to boost domestic demand," he added.
The non-manufacturing PMI, which measures activity in other areas including services and construction, came in at 49.7 in October, the data showed.
That was lower than a Bloomberg forecast of 50.0, and down from the 50.2 recorded in September.

Huo, the NBS statistician, said the drop was "influenced by factors such as a decline in (business) prosperity within certain service sectors," particularly the financial sector, but did not elaborate.
There was also a slowdown in construction activity compared to the previous month, Huo said.

2a63c1df51218aa1: AYER KEROH: Barisan Nasional supports the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) signed between the government and opposition MPs, with its chairman, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, saying similar arrangements should be extended to other political parties.

a7412ad3d096dc27: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 31 — Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s brother has stressed the urgent need for transparency in the domestic equity market, warning that Jakarta must “mitigate the MSCI issue” and demanding that corporate leaders immediately stop “deep frying” stocks.

“I’ve been tasked by the president to help ensure this doesn’t spiral out of control,” Hashim Djojohadikusumo said in Jakarta, speaking in his capacity as the president’s special envoy and advisory board chairman of the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (Kadin), according to Bloomberg.

“This is a very, very serious issue,” Hashim said. “Because if foreign investment pulls out of our stock market, the rupiah could weaken further. We’ll have to pay more for our foreign loans. This could become a disaster and catastrophe for the Indonesian economy.”

US index compiler MSCI Inc warned earlier this month that Indonesia could face a downgrade to standalone status, a severe sanction triggered by mounting concerns over opaque shareholding structures and coordinated trading in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.
The warnings have hammered sentiment on the Indonesia Stock Exchange, where the benchmark index has tumbled roughly 41 per cent this year, weighed down by a 3.5 per cent slide on Thursday.

In response to MSCI’s October 15 notice, Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority (OJK) announced penalties against more than a dozen entities involved in market manipulation. OJK head Friderica Widyasari Dewi confirmed on the sidelines of the Kadin forum that sanctioned firms have since paid IDR2.1 trillion (RM512 million) in fines, though the regulator has yet to disclose their identities.

Hashim addressed an audience comprising hundreds of business figures, including tycoons Anindya Bakrie and Franky Widjaja. Widjaja is the ultimate controlling shareholder of PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa, one of the entities under regulatory scrutiny.
His warning came days after President Prabowo asserted that “the Indonesian nation is not afraid of anyone and will not be intimidated.”
Hashim pressed market players to halt the local equivalent of saham gorengan, the coordinated churning and ramping of share prices detached from corporate fundamentals.

“Please stop deep frying stocks immediately because the government intends to take firm action,” Hashim said, cautioning that capital outflows triggered by a potential double downgrade could push the rupiah to 22,000 per US dollar. “This would have an extraordinarily negative political impact.”

Bank Indonesia Governor Destry Damayanti told reporters at the gathering that currency fluctuations reflect multiple dynamics, including global market sentiment. She noted that the central bank remains focused on ensuring currency stability to support real-sector expansion, emphasising that the rupiah is backed by solid underlying fundamentals.
Hashim added that the protracted equity slump directly hurts retail investors across the archipelago.

“There are 32.7 million Indonesian citizens who hold brokerage accounts — in other words, they’re investing through the stock market,” he said. “Well, the problem is that right now, those 32.7 million Indonesians are extremely dissatisfied with the situation. They’re unhappy because the value of their stocks has dropped.”
Hashim, an established conglomerate head who has long served as Prabowo’s key financial and political strategist, played a pivotal role in backing his brother’s path to the presidency.

64c205aac7cf6354: PARIS, Oct 31 — Global anti-money laundering watchdog the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) said Friday it had removed Monaco and three other countries from its “grey list”, two years after it put the principality among its territories requiring increased monitoring.
Bulgaria, Democratic Republic of Congo and the Ivory Coast were also removed from the list, the organisation said after a plenary meeting.
The countries had completed promised action plans “and will no longer be subject to the FATF’s increased monitoring process,” it added.
The Paris-based FATF monitors efforts by more than 200 countries and jurisdictions to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism.
Grey list nations are considered to have “strategic deficiencies” in countering money laundering and terrorist financing, while cooperating with the FATF to correct the problems.

Long known as a playground for the rich and famous, tiny Monaco, with a population of less than 40,000, attracts moneyed residents from around the world with its extremely favourable tax regime, with no income or wealth taxes.
The FATF said Monaco had made “significant progress” in strengthening the effectiveness of its efforts to counter money laundering and terrorist financing.

“This decision recognizes more than two years of concrete, rigorous and coordinated work by all of the State’s authorities and departments,” the head of Monaco’s government, Christophe Mirmand, said in a statement.
The FATF had urged the Mediterranean principality to boost resources for investigators and prosecutors and increase seizures of property suspected to derive from criminal activities.
It called for more effective cooperation on countering money laundering and terrorist financing, and for officials to send more requests to identify and seek the seizure of criminal assets abroad.
Monaco introduced an offence of presumed money laundering to facilitate the prosecution of cases involving suspicious funds.
It also boosted funding for its financial regulator and created a special unit in the public prosecutor’s office.
“We do not see this as a finish line: what matters now is what Monaco delivers over the long term,” Mirmand added.
Dozens of money-laundering probes were underway in 2025, and convictions rose from three in 2021 to 28 in 2025, according to Monaco’s authorities.
Bulgaria, which had been put on the grey list in 2023, also welcomed its removal.
This “means more confidence in our country, more investment and more jobs,” Prime Minister Roumen Radev said in a statement.
It will also facilitate Bulgaria’s international financial transfers, he added.
Democratic Republic of Congo had been on the grey list since 2022 and Ivory Coast since 2024.
The exit of the four countries leaves 18 on the FATF’s grey list, including Bosnia, Bolivia, Iraq, Syria, Yemen and the British Virgin islands.
Three countries are on the FATF’s black list of countries that are high risk for money laundering and terrorism financing: Iran, Myanmar and North Korea. — AFP

7d73457714d933a5: LONDON, Oct 31 — Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, estimates that assets worth US$6.3 billion (RM25.7 billion) were impacted by a hacking attack against the trading platform.

In France, Binance is suspected of having failed to meet its obligations regarding the oversight of client funds.
Having failed to obtain authorisation under the European Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) regulation, Binance recently announced a partial suspension of its operations within the European Union.
A secure technology?
Cryptocurrencies are based on a technology called blockchain, a digital ledger that records transactions and is designed to make falsification particularly difficult.
Transfers are authorised using “private keys” – long strings of characters kept secret. However, this does not fully protect funds from theft.
“Even when you think you are using one of the most robust exchanges in the world, it can still be hacked,” Stephane Ifrah, an analyst at Coinhouse, told AFP.
How can hackers still get in?
To gain access to private keys or the systems that authorise transfers, hackers can exploit a software vulnerability, deploy malicious software, or target individuals – for instance through phishing.
Some keys are stored on hardware wallets that are not connected to the internet.
However, these devices are not immune to attacks. Funds belonging to users of the French firm Ledger were stolen after malicious components were inserted into devices sold by a third-party retailer.
In the case of Binance, the investigation is pointing toward a “compromised” laptop of one of its engineers, in addition to “points of breach”, the platform said on X.
Who are the hackers?

While there has been no official confirmation, analyst firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic point to hackers linked to North Korea, specifically the group known as TraderTraitor or the “Lazarus Group”.
The amount purportedly stolen is four times the sum that the same hackers – according to the FBI – siphoned from the platform Bybit in February 2025.
That theft totalled US$1.5 billion, which at the time was the largest ever cryptocurrency heist.

According to Elliptic and Chainalysis, some of the funds stolen from Binance have been traced to the same pool of assets as those taken in a recent hack of the platform Bitget, which the victim attributed to Pyongyang.
Is it possible to recover the money?
Binance says that around US$3 billion of the affected crypto – nearly half the total amount affected – has been frozen with help from issuers and infrastructure partners.
But the freezing of assets does not mean the funds have been recovered.
According to Ifrah, the attackers could employ anonymisation tools, such as cryptocurrency “mixers” or “tumblers”, designed to make tracking the stolen assets more difficult.
Binance asserts that it will cover the losses resulting from the hack.
But as Ifrah states, “it is clear that there is no such thing as zero risk”. — AFP

8f9e81279e5a8c4d: From Moaz Nair
If you ever feel ignored at work, underappreciated by your friends or are generally invisible to the human eye, take comfort. You could be the Malaysian Indian People’s Party (MIPP) or Gerakan.
In the grand corporate hierarchy of Perikatan Nasional (PN), these two are the interns who don't get invited to the lunch table, yet somehow believe they are next in line for the CEO's position.
To say that MIPP and Gerakan bring no clout to PN is a profound insult to the word clout.

They are the political equivalents of plastic indoor plants – supposed to add a splash of "multiracial colour" to a very green room – except the plants have withered, the owners keep forgetting to water them and the landlords are currently trying to evict the entire building.

The political future of these minority component parties in PN has become one of the most ironic talking points in modern Malaysian politics. Critics, political analysts and observers frequently debate their position, although "debate" might be too active a word. It is more akin to watching two passengers argue over who gets the window seat on a bus that has already driven off a cliff.
MIPP: from bold newcomers to zero-vote club

Let’s start with MIPP, the bold newcomers whose political future in PN is currently the hottest topic among three guys at a coffee shop. MIPP entered the scene with the explosive energy of a damp firecracker. At its grand electoral debut in Johor, it contested five seats and managed a spectacular, flawless clean sweep of losing their deposits in all five.

MIPP’s standing within a major coalition remains precarious precisely because it has demonstrated a rare, mathematically impressive lack of an independent base. Yet, MIPP’s confidence remains unshaken by minor details like numerical reality.

Recently, the party announced it would completely sit out the Nov 14 Melaka state election after seat distribution talks with the PN leadership broke down. The official reason? President P Punithan bravely declared that the party refuses to compromise its dignity or accept "irrelevant" seats just to field candidates.

Translation: PN offered it a constituency consisting entirely of three palm trees and a stray cat, and MIPP chose "dignity" over another hefty loss of deposit. This breakdown signals deep friction over how minority component parties are treated by the dominant Malay-Muslim parties in PN.

The ideological mismatch here is staggering. MIPP is trying to pitch a minority-interest narrative in a coalition heavily dominated by PAS’s religious and conservative Malay narratives. It’s like trying to sell vegan burgers at a Texas steakhouse and acting surprised when the chef throws a spatula at you. It is incredibly difficult for a minority-interest party like MIPP to gain genuine traction among non-Muslim voters while standing next to politicians who view secularism as a design flaw.

Ultimately, MIPP’s decision to bypass Melaka highlights the ongoing, tragicomic struggle for minor non-Malay component parties to find an equal voice in a house that doesn't even know they are in the room.
Gerakan: master of the secular submissive

Then we have Gerakan, the veteran master of political irrelevance. The argument that Gerakan has no future in PN is a view increasingly shared by political analysts, critics, and even internal party factions who have grown tired of buying antacids in bulk.

Political observers highlight several compounding crises that threaten Gerakan's long-term viability in the coalition. First and foremost is its utter inability to attract non-Malay voters. Gerakan originally joined PN to serve as its non-Malay face, a bridge to the cynical urban electorate. Instead, it has become a cautionary tale, repeatedly failing to win over non-Malay voters from Pakatan Harapan, particularly DAP.

This has trapped it in the "shadow dilemma" – a polite academic term for operating entirely in the shadow of its larger partners, PAS and Bersatu. Because Gerakan brings minimal electoral data or seat victories to the table, its leverage in PN is roughly equivalent to a discount voucher that expired during the Asian financial crisis.

The ideological friction between Gerakan’s secular principles and PAS’s Islamic stance peaked hilariously during the school brewery donation saga. When PAS attacked the fund-raising, Gerakan deputy president Oh Tong Keong threatened to exit the coalition over "extreme" demands. PAS responded with a collective yawn, and Gerakan naturally stayed – proving that its red lines are drawn in invisible ink.

Naturally, this masterclass in political submission has triggered an internal rebellion. High-profile departures – such as the resignation of 31-year veteran and party treasurer Hng Chee Wey – underscore a growing internal revolt against sacrificing core principles for political expediency. These exits expose deep cracks under president Dominic Lau, as grassroots members grow tired of watching their leadership nod politely while being publicly sidelined.
PN's burning house

To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire. The broader PN coalition is undergoing severe structural shocks, with PAS announcing the end of its political cooperation with Bersatu, triggering a chaotic power struggle and the sudden resignation of top PN leadership.

The Registrar of Societies even ordered the coalition's deregistration, and while a temporary court reprieve saved it from legal oblivion, persistent internal rifts cloud the bloc's political future. It is a civil war where the big boys are throwing live grenades, and Gerakan and MIPP are caught in the crossfire armed with plastic cutlery.

What is Gerakan’s next move? Political analysts suggest that leaving the coalition may be a risk worth taking compared to staying and enduring further humiliation. Yet, Lau has indicated that Gerakan is trying to pivot by backing a broader PN-Barisan Nasional electoral tie-up for future stability.

Yes, you read that correctly. While PN is on the verge of structural collapse and PAS is actively exploring independent realignments with Umno, Gerakan is trying to build a bridge to a party that doesn't know it exists, using a blueprint that is already out of date.
Conclusion

Gerakan risks being completely left behind unless it thoroughly recalibrates its political alignment. But that would require a sense of direction, and right now, both Gerakan and MIPP seem perfectly content to sit in the back seat of a driverless car heading straight towards a cliff, arguing over who gets to hold the auxiliary cable.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

2286dcf6a47eca45: NEW YORK, Oct 31 — Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a “complex attack” that affected around US$6.3 billion (RM25.7b) in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist, with investigators pointing to hackers linked to North Korea.

Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had “high confidence” that the attack was orchestrated by a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor, the same group blamed for the US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
Another analytics firm, Elliptic, also attributed the attack to North Korea-linked hackers, according to industry outlet CoinDesk.

TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for “The Interview,” a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach,” contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X.

The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around US$6.3 billion,” four times the amount taken in the Bybit hack, the biggest cyberattack of its kind until now.

Binance warned the figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.”
It said around US$3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
Customers’ account balances have not been touched, but they cannot move funds off the platform while withdrawals remain suspended.
Binance initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals but later said deposits were unaffected. At about 0900 GMT Friday, it said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours.

President Donald Trump said Friday the United States was looking into the hack, and the FBI said it was “engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity” and was ready to investigate.
Fund freeze

The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorized party to execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete.
The unauthorized withdrawals drained Binance’s hot wallets – the online wallets the exchange uses to process customer transfers – across several blockchains, according to CoinDesk.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.”
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether, a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT, said his firm froze about US$1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than US$800 million in USDC.
USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins,” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar.
Crypto prices tumble
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins.
Bitcoin plunged nearly five per cent after the news, falling overnight to around US$76,400, its lowest level since mid-September, before recovering slightly to trade at about US$77,300.
Ethereum dropped nearly six per cent, while BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent.

The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. — AFP

68f2fe60ad7543ba: Washington’s decision to order non-emergency American diplomatic personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia is more than a precautionary measure. It signals a dangerous deterioration in the security environment of West Asia.
For Malaysia, the implications are immediate, strategic and potentially costly.

Saudi Arabia is not merely another oil-producing country. It is a pivotal power in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the custodian of Islam’s two holiest cities and an indispensable pillar of global energy security.
When Washington begins withdrawing diplomatic personnel from Riyadh, Kuala Lumpur must pay attention.
The decision follows increasingly audacious attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi airports, energy installations and civilian infrastructure.
The recent targeting of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield demonstrates how asymmetric warfare can undermine even a militarily sophisticated state.

Saudi Arabia possesses advanced Western weapons systems, extensive financial resources and powerful international partnerships. Yet relatively inexpensive drones and missiles continue to penetrate or challenge its defensive arrangements.
This carries five important lessons for Malaysia.
First, energy security cannot be separated from national security.
Although Malaysia produces petroleum and natural gas, its economy remains vulnerable to disruptions in global energy markets.
Higher transportation costs, expensive imported industrial inputs and renewed inflationary pressures could weaken domestic purchasing power.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government has worked to preserve economic stability amid considerable international uncertainty.
A prolonged crisis in Saudi Arabia could undermine these efforts, especially if disruptions spread across the Persian Gulf and Red Sea.
Second, maritime security must be understood as an interconnected strategic system.
The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are indispensable arteries of international commerce.
If both become increasingly dangerous, shipping companies will face higher insurance premiums, longer journeys and mounting operational costs.
Malaysia, strategically positioned along the Strait of Malacca, cannot remain insulated from these developments.
Disruptions in West Asia can eventually affect Malaysian ports, manufacturers, exporters and consumers.
Third, the Houthis have demonstrated the growing effectiveness of asymmetric warfare.
Military superiority no longer guarantees comprehensive security.
Drones, missiles, cyberattacks and sabotage can inflict enormous economic damage without requiring conventional military parity.
Malaysia and Asean must therefore strengthen the protection of airports, ports, energy installations and communications networks.
The strategic lesson is straightforward: resilience matters as much as deterrence.
Fourth, Saudi instability carries serious implications for Malaysian pilgrims.
Mecca and Madinah remain central to the religious lives of Malaysian Muslims.
Any deterioration in aviation security or airport operations could complicate haj and umrah arrangements.
Wisma Putra, Tabung Haji and Malaysia’s diplomatic missions must strengthen contingency planning, particularly regarding evacuation procedures, flight disruptions and consular assistance.
The safety of Malaysian citizens must remain paramount.
Fifth, the American decision exposes the limitations of excessive dependence on external security guarantees.

The United States remains militarily formidable. Nevertheless, its decision to reduce diplomatic exposure demonstrates that even Washington cannot eliminate every security threat confronting its allies.
Malaysia must therefore deepen its strategic relationships with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, China and other influential powers.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

256141e19a66337a: Dalam dunia moden, masyarakat sering merasakan mereka bebas membentuk pendapat sendiri. Namun, seperti dihujahkan oleh Edward S Herman dan Noam Chomsky dalam karya penting Manufacturing Consent (1988), pendapat umum sebenarnya dibentuk melalui hubungan rapat antara elit politik, elit korporat dan pemilik media.

Herman & Chomsky menunjukkan media arus perdana tidak benar-benar bebas; sebaliknya, ia mengikuti struktur kepentingan pemilik, pengiklan, kerajaan, dan rangkaian ekonomi-politik yang mengawal aliran maklumat. Apabila masyarakat bersandar kepada elit kerajaan, agensi dan tokoh berpengaruh, keputusan menjadi lebih mudah ‘diurus’ kerana rakyat bergantung kepada sumber yang sudah dianggap sah dan berautoriti.
Jika pada era lama pemilik media ialah syarikat akhbar, konglomerat penyiaran dan stesen televisyen nasional, hari ini ‘pemilik media’ telah berubah wajah menjadi pemilik platform digital.

Herman & Chomsky menekankan sesiapa yang menguasai infrastruktur penyampaian maklumat akan menguasai ruang fikir masyarakat. Dalam konteks abad ke-21, kuasa itu bukan lagi dimonopoli oleh kerajaan atau syarikat media tradisional, tetapi oleh gergasi digital seperti Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp), Google (YouTube), X (Twitter), TikTok, dan aplikasi mesej peribadi seperti Telegram.
Mereka bukan sahaja menyebar kandungan, tetapi mengawal algoritma iaitu sistem yang menentukan apa yang rakyat lihat, baca dan bincangkan setiap hari.

Inilah versi baharu manufacturing consent dalam era digital: persetujuan tidak lagi dibentuk melalui editorial akhbar, tetapi melalui newsfeed, trending list dan algoritma cadangan yang direka untuk memaksimumkan masa tontonan.

Sebagai contoh, Facebook boleh mengangkat isu tertentu sehingga kelihatan seperti ‘suara rakyat’, walaupun ia sebenarnya digerakkan oleh kumpulan kecil belakang tabir yang mengeksploitasi sistem perkongsian. Begitu juga YouTube, yang boleh mempercepatkan penyebaran ideologi tertentu melalui cadangan video yang memerangkap pengguna dalam echo chamber.

Walaupun kerajaan masih mempunyai kuasa kawalan, yang menurut saya terhad kepada kandungan. Mereka kini bergantung pula kepada platform digital untuk menjangkau rakyat, menjadikan pemilik platform sebagai rakan strategik atau ancaman senyap dalam pembentukan pendapat umum.

Hubungan ini dapat dilihat dalam pilihan raya moden. Di Amerika Syarikat, kempen Donald Trump 2016 bergantung kepada Facebook Ads yang menyasarkan kelompok tertentu dengan mesej emosi, membuktikan bahawa pemilik data kini lebih berpengaruh daripada pemilik media tradisional.

Di Malaysia, penyebaran naratif politik di TikTok menjelang PRU15 menunjukkan bagaimana anak muda membina pandangan politik bukan daripada ucapan rasmi, tetapi daripada video pendek yang dikuasai algoritma. Ini menunjukkan kuasa mengurus masyarakat kini bergantung kepada gabungan kerajaan + elit korporat + pemilik platform digital, bukannya kerajaan sahaja.
Secara keseluruhan, apabila masyarakat terlalu bersandar kepada elit berkuasa baik kerajaan, media tradisional atau pemilik digital maka proses membuat keputusan menjadi lebih mudah dimanipulasi.

Masyarakat percaya kerana mereka menganggap sumber-sumber ini ‘natural’ dan neutral, sedangkan Herman & Chomsky membuktikan setiap sistem media sebenarnya mempunyai struktur kepentingan yang tersusun. Dalam era digital hari ini, propaganda menjadi lebih halus kerana ia bukan lagi disampaikan oleh editor manusia, tetapi oleh algoritma yang memutuskan apa yang wajar ditonton.
Pemahaman ini penting supaya masyarakat sedar bahawa ‘kemudahan membuat keputusan’ selalunya datang dengan harga: penyerahan sebahagian kebebasan berfikir kepada elit yang mengawal aliran maklumat.
Bagaimana ekosistem ini mempengaruhi fikiran dan tindakan masyarakat

Ekosistem yang dibina oleh kerajaan, pemilik media tradisional dan pemilik platform digital hari ini membentuk satu sistem pengaruh yang hampir total. Masyarakat yang bergantung pada sumber-sumber rasmi dan platform digital untuk memahami dunia akan mengikuti aliran maklumat yang telah ‘ditapis’ sebelum sampai kepada mereka.

Dalam kerangka Herman & Chomsky, ini ialah proses penyusunan agenda di mana apa yang dianggap penting oleh rakyat sebenarnya ditentukan oleh struktur kuasa di belakang media. Platform digital menambah satu lapisan baharu: maklumat bukan sahaja disaring oleh pemilik media, tetapi dipilih oleh algoritma yang mengutamakan interaksi popular dan bukan atas agenda kepentingan negara.
Akibatnya, isu yang paling banyak mendapat perhatian bukanlah isu yang paling penting, tetapi isu yang paling menguntungkan dari segi trafik dan emosi.

Ekosistem ini mempengaruhi cara masyarakat berfikir dengan mencipta ilusi bahawa maklumat datang secara organik, sedangkan ia sebenarnya hasil kawalan sistemik. Contohnya, seseorang mungkin percaya sesuatu isu ‘hangat dibincangkan rakyat’ kerana ia tular di TikTok, walhal algoritma hanya menolak kandungan serupa berulang kali sehingga mencipta kesan majoriti palsu.

Ini disebut Herman & Chomsky sebagai manufactured perception, persepsi yang dibuat, bukan dilahirkan secara semula jadi. Begitu juga dalam konteks politik: apabila naratif tertentu diulang melalui media arus perdana dan disokong oleh kemunculan semula video pendek di laman sosial, masyarakat mula melihat naratif itu sebagai ‘kebenaran kolektif’. Mereka percaya bukan kerana bukti, tetapi kerana kekerapan dan kebiasaan.

Ekosistem ini juga mempengaruhi emosi kolektif. Kerajaan mungkin menetapkan nada optimistik seperti ‘ekonomi stabil’, media tradisional mengulanginya melalui laporan rasmi, dan platform digital memanjangkan emosi itu melalui konten yang dipromosikan oleh algoritma seperti infografik, meme, video pendek, atau klip ucapan pemimpin. Pada masa sama, algoritma meminggirkan suara yang dianggap tidak menguntungkan atau bertentangan dengan arus popular.

Apabila masyarakat hanya dibenarkan melihat satu sisi, mereka percaya itulah keseluruhan cerita. Keadaan ini menjadikan propaganda lebih efisien kerana ia tidak memaksa masyarakat menerima sesuatu naratif, tetapi membentuk persekitaran maklumat yang membuatkan naratif itu kelihatan seperti pilihan paling logik.

Selain fikiran dan emosi, ekosistem digital juga mempengaruhi tingkah laku. Di Malaysia, kita dapat lihat bagaimana pola pengundian anak muda berubah secara drastik apabila mereka terdedah kepada video politik TikTok dan bukan kerana hujah rasional, tetapi kerana naratif visual yang dikuatkan oleh algoritma.

Di peringkat global, kempen Trump 2016 dan Brexit menunjukkan bagaimana data pengguna digunakan untuk menyasarkan mesej individu mengikut ketakutan, minat dan kelemahan masing-masing. Apabila algoritma mengetahui apa yang mencetuskan kemarahan, ketakutan atau harapan seseorang, ia boleh mempengaruhi tindakannya tanpa individu itu sedar mereka sedang dipengaruhi.

Akhirnya, ekosistem ini menjadikan masyarakat lebih mudah diurus. Herman & Chomsky menyebut media moden sebagai ‘sistem propaganda’ yang tidak kelihatan seperti propaganda kerana ia berfungsi dalam suasana kebebasan. Dalam era digital, sistem ini menjadi lebih kuat: masyarakat percaya mereka bebas memilih, tetapi pilihan mereka telah dibentuk oleh infrastruktur maklumat yang dikuasai oleh kerajaan, pemilik media, dan pemilik platform digital global.

Kesimpulannya, apabila aliran maklumat dikawal oleh jaringan elit ini, masyarakat bukan sahaja terpengaruh, malah diarahkan tanpa sedar untuk berfikir, merasa dan bertindak mengikut kepentingan pihak yang menguasai sistem.

0a7c6a7f6988f770: In calling on Malaysians to reject the politics of hatred based on race and religion on Oct 25, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said some people were attempting to “distort history by claiming that this country can only be saved through the victory of a single race”.
“If our ancestors succeeded in building the Melaka Malay Sultanate into a great empire, we can do the same through peace, unity among all quarters, and sound development strategies,” he said.
I couldn’t agree more. And history proves him right.

In recent decades the tension over whose country this is has taken on a life of its own, with those arguing for ketuanan Melayu or calling non-Malays pendatang gaining in strength. So much so that it has put many non-Malay citizens on the defensive.
It is as if Malay political strength and cosmopolitan composition are rivals for the same space.
They need not be, as Melaka’s history shows.

For roughly a century, the most important port in the Malay world was simultaneously the most thoroughly Malay polity in the region and one of the most diverse places on earth. Both facts were true at once. Neither diluted the other.

The Sultanate of Melaka was unambiguously Malay and Islamic. The court spoke Malay, kept Malay adat, drew its ceremonial rituals from Hindu-derived concepts filtered through centuries of courtly tradition, and derived legitimacy from control of the Strait of Melaka.

And yet the city’s population was staggering in its variety. Tomé Pires, writing within living memory of the sultanate’s fall, described traders from around the world who spoke somewhere around eighty-four languages in the port.

Gujarati Muslim traders and Tamil merchants from India traded here; Hokkien and Cantonese-speaking Chinese merchants ran warehouses; and Javanese, Siamese, Cham, Ryukyuan, Arab, Persian and Filipino traders also maintained quarters here.
There were resident communities with temples, mosques, shrines and headmen of their own.
This diversity was not incidental to Melakan power. It was Melakan power. The sultanate’s wealth came from being the place where the South China Sea met the Indian Ocean.

And that could only work if an Indian Muslim or Tamil merchant, a junk owner from Quanzhou and a pepper shipper from Java could all find or agree on the same weights, the same credit practices and the same language of contract.
Cosmopolitanism was not a value Melaka upheld. It was the economic base.

Melaka’s answer to governing this population was administrative rather than ideological. The state appointed a Shahbandar — the chief port master — to oversee all traders and revenue. The Shahbandar managed distinct trading quarters, registered merchants, collected taxes, settled internal disputes, and liaised with the government.

In practice this gave each community customary autonomy over its own affairs (marriage, inheritance, temple and mosque management), while the Bendahara handled internal Malay affairs. All commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction, however, rested with the sultanate.

The arrangement deserves attention precisely because it looks superficially like what colonial administrators later built and what Malaysian coalition politics later imitated — separate channels for separate communities. But the difference is structural, and it matters for how we think about unity today.

Under colonial rule, communal separation was the point. British policy froze categories through census classification, partitioned schooling by language, segregated employment by race, and treated intermixture as a management problem. Communities coexisted economically while remaining socially sealed, held together from above by an administration that belonged to none of them.

Melaka’s system separated for the purpose of incorporation. The Shahbandar registered you so you could trade, marry, inherit and litigate inside Melaka’s order. The Undang-Undang Melaka and the maritime code recognised community customs while reserving commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction to the state.
Malay was the lingua franca of the market and the court, and participation in that common life was the price and the reward of belonging.

Movement across lines was expected and routine. Chinese traders married locally and produced Baba-Nyonya culture. Indian Muslims settled into quarters that became permanent neighbourhoods, as did the Tamil merchants. And Arab Syed families entered Malay genealogies.
Conversion to Islam opened the fullest paths into the elite, and did so without erasing the commercial networks converts had brought with them.

Unity here meant a shared sovereign frame, a shared commercial language and a shared legal horizon — not shared blood, shared schooling or shared culture. Diversity was not accommodated at the margin. It was administered at the centre.

Against this record, the claim that non-Malay presence in the peninsula is a colonial residue awaiting digestion does not survive contact with the evidence. The ancestors of today’s Malaysian Chinese and Malaysian Indian communities were not confined to nineteenth-century steamships.

Long before Penang, Singapore and Melaka passed to Britain, there were resident Chinese, Tamil, Indian Muslim, Gujarati and Arab populations under Malay sovereignty here. They were registered, taxed, and adjudicated; and they even intermarried.
They were not guests awaiting permanent permission and the Shahbandar was not a manager of ethnicities.
That historical fact dismantles the foundational premise of ethnic exclusivism — that Malayness and non-Malay residence are, in principle, incompatible claims on the same land.
Five hundred years of Malay statecraft say otherwise, in Jawi script, in the records of a Malay court.

Honesty, however, requires stating the limits. Melaka was a transit entrepôt with a small population, perhaps tens of thousands, many of them sojourners, governed as subjects rather than citizens, and ranked by status and religion in ways no modern Malaysian would want restored.

So Melaka is not a blueprint. Nobody should propose reviving the Shahbandar offices. But it is something more useful than a blueprint: it is a refutation. It removes the alibi. If exclusion is defended on the grounds that Malay civilisation has always been exclusive, the fifteenth-century record contradicts the defence.
If assimilation is defended on the grounds that diversity requires uniformity to be governable, the fifteenth-century record contradicts that too.

What survives the comparison is a definition. Melaka shows that this region produced a working model of unity in diversity in which unity meant shared sovereignty, shared law and shared language, while diversity meant real autonomy of custom, belief and association.
The unity did not require the diversity to dissolve. The diversity did not threaten the unity.
This is an opportune time to remember this historical fact, as voters prepare to go to the polls in Melaka next month.

Some politicians will surely tell voters that they must choose between affirming Malay identity and embracing the country’s plural character; that they must unite to save their race or religion. Others may say voters need to come together to defend their rights.

The city’s own history says the choice being thrown at them was invented by colonial administrators who preferred divided subjects to a mixed populace. Before the colonialists came, the most successful Malay state in history proved the two were never opposites.

It would be asking a great deal of a banner-waving election season to engage with that. But the evidence sits there, in plain sight, in the very state being fought over — and it is worth saying out loud, in Melaka, before the voting: this country’s diversity is not a problem Malay civilisation inherited from outsiders. It is an achievement Malay civilisation once mastered.

ad16ca4f20c10fb9: NEW YORK, Oct 31 — Nvidia’s US$3 billion (RM12 billion) investment in Meta’s share sale, announced Tuesday, is the latest addition to a portfolio of stakes, loans and guarantees that has made the chip giant what some analysts describe as the central bank of the artificial intelligence boom.
The galaxy of deals has helped keep demand running high for Nvidia’s processors, which power vast data centres around the world and are the central ingredient of the AI revolution.
That demand has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company by market capitalisation and turned chief executive Jensen Huang into AI’s kingmaker.
But the investments have raised a nagging question among some doubters on Wall Street: is Nvidia helping to inflate an AI bubble?
What is Nvidia investing in?
Nvidia has taken stakes in leading AI developers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI, now part of SpaceX.
It has also invested in “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent out computing power built on Nvidia chips.

Its bets extend well beyond the United States. In Europe, Nvidia has backed French AI developer Mistral and British self-driving startup Wayve. In Asia, it has teamed up with South Korea’s SK Group to build data centres.
Beyond equity, the company has offered financial backstops, acting as a customer of last resort.
In CoreWeave’s case, Nvidia committed to buy up to US$6.3 billion of unused computing capacity if no other customer takes it.
Nvidia also has around US$36 billion in cloud backstops and a guarantee of up to US$105 billion linked to an OpenAI data centre, according to US media.
Why is Nvidia doing this?
Experts say Nvidia’s enormous profits give it few better options.
“They’re essentially becoming a bank,” said Michael Cusumano, a professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management.
“Channeling it back to infrastructure investment tied to purchases of Nvidia equipment is a smart thing.”
He said the alternatives were less attractive.
Running its own data centers would put Nvidia in competition with its biggest customers “and that might also trigger a whole bunch of antitrust complaints,” Cusumano added.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia identifies parts of the AI ecosystem that are not investing enough and puts money into them to fill the gaps.
“It’s unprecedented, but it appears to be working,” he said.
Huang has defended the approach, arguing that frontier AI labs are the first generation of startups that need tens of billions of dollars to get started, not just millions.
Nvidia’s investments effectively give those companies more time to succeed.
Is it ‘circular’ financing?
Critics have compared the deals to the dot-com era, when companies inflated their growth by investing in startups that then bought their products.
“There is nothing intrinsically wrong with Nvidia helping its clients,” said Paulo Carvão, a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School.
“But the closer these relationships are, the harder it is for one to assess true sustainable demand.”
Luria said not all demand was equal.

“If Nvidia gives CoreWeave money to turn around and buy Nvidia chips, that’s not as good as Microsoft buying Nvidia chips because they have a customer in OpenAI that has a customer in an enterprise technology that’s willing to pay for it,” he said.
What are the risks?
The main concern is concentration. Two direct customers accounted for 22 percent and 14 per cent of Nvidia’s revenue in its 2026 fiscal year, according to the company’s annual report.
Carvão said the web of overlapping investments increases the risk of contagion if a weaker company such as CoreWeave runs into trouble.
“If AI demand disappoints, spending cuts could hit chipmakers, data-center builders and their financiers at once,” he said.

Those concerns have grown this month. Shares of several Nvidia-linked neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, fell at least 30 per cent in October amid worries about tighter credit for AI projects.
Carvão noted that the market for AI chips remains limited by supply. He estimated demand would keep growing for another 12 to 18 months before it begins to level off.
Cusumano said he expected high demand for Nvidia chips to continue for three to five years. — AFP
14797c52cd6d8406: MUMBAI: Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries on Friday reported its highest ever quarterly revenue, saying net profit rose 41% in the third quarter, helped by strong performances from its core oil-to-chemicals arm and digital services division.

Reliance's July-September numbers come days after the impressive debut of Jio Platforms, the conglomerate's digital services arm, which raised more than US$3 billion in the country's biggest initial public offering earlier this week.
The retail-to-refining giant led by billionaire tycoon Mukesh Ambani is India's most valuable company by market capitalisation.
The conglomerate reported revenue of 3.62 trillion rupees (US$38 billion), up 27.8% year-on-year and its highest ever quarterly sales figure, according to a company statement.
Reliance has aggressively expanded into telecom and green energy businesses over the last decade, but it still relies on its traditional oil business for profits.
The conglomerate owns and operates the world's largest refinery complex in the eastern Indian state of Gujarat.
The sector has faced multiple challenges, with the ongoing Middle East conflict affecting supplies, but Reliance has managed to diversify crude imports.
Reliance "delivered a strong performance despite a complex operating environment", Ambani said in the statement.
"Our ability to optimise feedstock sourcing and product placement along with operations across the value chain enabled us to improve margin capture," Ambani added.
Jio's strong listing has also pushed the growth.
Launched a decade ago, Jio's wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

With more than 530 million subscribers, the firm currently makes most of its money from telecoms, but has expanded in recent years into newer areas including digital services and artificial intelligence.
Analysts see Jio as the key to Reliance's strategy to evolve beyond its traditional business and a touchstone of its future tech ambitions.
Ambani said Reliance has set "multiple global benchmarks."
"It demonstrates the depth of confidence investors place in Jio’s solid foundation and strong growth visibility," he added.

328e11e7c76814d7: NEW YORK: US stocks tumbled on Friday, with the Nasdaq suffering its largest one-day percentage drop since June 5 following disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon, which amplified growing worries surrounding AI-related companies' massive spending on the nascent technology.
All three major US stock indexes slumped, with the Nasdaq sliding 2.9%. The tech-heavy index has dropped 7.8% from its all-time closing high reached on Oct 6.
The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday. While Amazon pared losses as the session progressed, Intel shares plunged 28.6%.

Chip stocks veered sharply lower, with Nvidia down 4.2% and AMD sliding 10.9%. The broader chips index shed 7.2%, slumping to a monthly loss of more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP dropped 10.8% and 9.6%, respectively.

"It's fair to say that this week, not just today, has been very much about the future of AI and what that's going to look like, whether there will be a positive return on investment and if so, how quickly," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York.

"Companies that are performing and meeting the very lofty expectations that have been set are doing well," Pursche added. "Those that are falling short and seem to be missing the mark or not executing as expected are getting punished."
All three main equity indexes closed lower on the week. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq logged monthly losses, while the Dow exited October with a gain.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31, the S&P 500 lost 140.32 points, or 1.82%, to 7,580.07 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.86%, to 25,437.00.
The S&P 500 tech sector posted its largest monthly percentage loss since March 2025, and communication services registered its biggest monthly drop since April 2022.
Third-quarter earnings season has passed the halfway mark, with 299 companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 82% have beaten consensus expectations, according to LSEG data.
Analysts now expect third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 31.6%, year-on-year, per LSEG.

Oil supermajors Exxon Mobil and Chevron both beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from soaring profit margins as a result of energy supply disruptions arising from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine. The stocks gained 2.2% and 2.8%, respectively.
Starbucks dipped 1.8% after the coffee chain forecast an annual revenue decline due to its divestiture of its Chinese business.

Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy, and Robinhoon fell between 7.2% and 10.6% in the wake of reports that hackers stole US$6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.8-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 169 new highs and 377 new lows on the NYSE.
On the Nasdaq, 1,196 stocks rose and 3,622 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.03-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 43 new 52-week highs and 5 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 70 new highs and 355 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 19.87 billion shares, compared with the 17.26 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.
