028d5ff4b1d516d0: An Exile Hub fellow shares their personal experiences and reflections
Originally published on Global Voices
Image from Exile Hub. Used with permission.

Exile Hub is one of Global Voices’ partners in Southeast Asia, emerging in response to the 2021 coup in Myanmar, and focusing on empowering journalists and human rights defenders. This article by a fellow of Exile Hub was published on August 15, 2026, and an edited version is republished under a content partnership agreement.
“Can I keep doing this work?”
I have asked myself that question more times than I can count.
When I first entered journalism as a young person, I was full of energy, conviction, and dreams. I believed journalism was a way to uncover the truth and to make sure people’s voices were heard.
Four years later, I began to realize that somewhere along the way, I was slowly losing parts of myself.
When I was 19, I never imagined that the career I chose would become both my livelihood and one of the reasons the road home would feel so far away.

In the early days of the 2021 revolution in Myanmar, I took part in protests. As the security situation deteriorated, I had to leave home. Eventually, I found myself in Mae Sot, a small town along the Thai–Myanmar border. There, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to study journalism for free.

I had loved writing since I was young. I started with short news pieces, then moved on to feature stories and video reporting, and eventually became a news presenter. I was proud to call myself a journalist. I was so proud, in fact, that I never used a pen name. I reported under my real name.
One of the first lessons I learned in journalism was simple: don’t put your own emotions into the story. But over time, I learned something else. Journalists are human too.
When other people’s pain becomes part of you
Sometimes I would call a source for an interview and listen as they described what had happened to them. Their pain would stay with me.
My responsibility was to listen carefully and then find the words to make their experiences visible to others. But sometimes, carrying their stories felt like carrying the pain twice.
After some interviews, I would put down my phone, open my laptop, and stare at the screen. No words would come.
I remember once speaking with a source just before mealtime. My stomach told me I was hungry, but after hearing their story, there was a heaviness in my chest, and I could not eat.
As these experiences accumulated, something began to change.
Eventually, I stopped crying.
I could finish an interview and immediately continue with the next task. But it wasn’t because the stories no longer affected me.
I had simply become numb.

And that numbness slowly changed me without my realizing it. I became tired more easily. I became irritable. I overthought things. My mood sank, and even my relationships with other people began to suffer.
Yet there was something strange about all of this.
On the days when I picked up my camera bag, carried my tripod, and went out into the field, some of that exhaustion disappeared.
Walking along windy roads, meeting people and listening to their lives, I would suddenly remember:
I still love this work.
And that’s why I couldn’t quite let it go.
When passion is not enough
COVID-19 and Myanmar’s political upheaval interrupted my education. Journalism became my livelihood, and surviving from one day to the next left little space to think seriously about my own future.
Eventually, one question began following me almost every day: What will become of me?
I became afraid that nothing would.
At the same time, media organizations were losing funding. Programs were closing. Journalists were losing their jobs.
When one of the programs I worked for ended, I became unemployed for around seven months.
It was one of the hardest periods of my life.
I told myself that if I could not find another job in journalism within a little over a year, I would change careers completely.
Fortunately, I eventually found my way back, working again as both a reporter and news presenter.
I continue because I genuinely love this work.
But love alone does not make the realities of life in exile easier. The income is not always enough to build a stable life.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
On the days when I desperately want to go home, I cannot.
Even if I cannot return myself, I wish I could bring my family to visit me. But financially, that is not always possible either.
I want to see the people I love. I want to eat my mother’s cooking. I miss the smell of home.
Most of all, I miss my mother.
She raised me by herself, and as she grows older, I want to be able to care for her in return. One of my deepest fears is that something will happen to her before I have the chance to see her again.
That distance makes an already exhausting life in exile even heavier.
When the mind begins to affect the body
At one point, I tried counseling.
But each session cost more than THB 800 (USD 24). I could not afford to continue for the long term, so eventually I stopped.
Over time, the emotional pressure began affecting my physical health as well. I was hospitalized twice, both times in serious conditions.
Being hospitalized in another country is difficult enough, even when you can afford it. When money is already tight, the anxiety becomes even greater.
After those experiences, I stopped trying to transform my life all at once.
Instead, I started small.
I learned to be grateful that I was alive today.
If the weather was beautiful, I appreciated it.
If I finished one task, I allowed myself to feel proud of it.
I would be lying if I said I no longer worry about where I will be in five or ten years — I still do.
But I am trying to spend less time living inside an uncertain future and more time doing the best I can with the day in front of me.
I still sometimes struggle in crowded places. There are moments when breathing becomes difficult, or my emotions change quickly.
And yet, strangely, when I am out reporting, I can become completely absorbed in the work and somehow manage.
The difference now is that I have learned to accept these parts of myself rather than constantly fight against them.
I have also learned something else:
We cannot carry everything alone.
Having someone who listens, someone who cares, someone who simply asks, “Are you okay?” can sometimes feel like medicine for the mind.
Still here, still trying
When I first entered journalism, I was simply a young person who wanted to write the truth.
Four years later, after witnessing so many painful stories, I have learned that telling other people’s stories also requires learning how to care for myself.
I still do not know what my future will look like.
I do not know when the road will take me home.
But there is one thing I have come to believe:
“As long as we are still alive, there is still something we can try.”
So I keep going with that belief.
I try to spend more time with the people who have cared for me and held me up when things became difficult. I try to appreciate them while they are still beside me.
And through all the days when I long to go home, I am still trying to survive in both of the identities I carry: as a journalist and as a human being.
Written by Exile Hub

8b3ed8665efbf0d7: Stenko Vlad/Shutterstock A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11. “I’m so angry that porn is so loved, and I’m so angry at myself for thinking that it was ok,” she said. Eilish became addicted to porn, and it led to problems. “The first few times I had sex, I was not saying no to things that were not good,” she said. She had nightmares because the content she was watching was so violent and abusive. Online porn is a multi-million dollar business, driven by algorithms designed to keep people clicking for more. These algorithms push more and more extreme content, often for free, to people who didn’t go searching for it. This can include strangulation, exploitation or incest porn, that’s often misogynistic and racist too. “If you take incest and strangulation, we can look at content studies from the 1980s, for example, when there was hardly any of that material,” Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University in the UK, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast. “Today both incest and strangulation becomes mainstream.” In the UK, the government will ban the possession and publication of incest and strangulation porn from early November. McGlynn, who worked with civil society groups to push the regulation of extreme content, says it’s a “huge step” that sends a message about the harms of “normalising sexual violence”. McGlynn, who has written a recent book about the rise of extreme porn, says large online porn platforms are pushing people towards more and more extreme content. Their business model is to keep you engaged. They want us on the platform for as long as possible, and the way to do that is to feed you more content, not necessarily what you were looking for, but also, the more extreme, the more polarising, the more shocking content … unfortunately, that seems to be what our kind of base instincts go for and what does actually engage us to keep us searching. McGlynn says an abundance of extreme and violent porn is shaping the sex lives of young people, and it can lead to an increased risk of problematic behaviour. There’s a study that followed 16,000 young people, showing that high porn use, particularly at a young age, is a big risk factor in problematic sexual behaviour of young teenage boys. And there’s studies in Australia and the US … showing that the more porn they watch, the more strangulation they see, and then the more they identify that they act out the strangulation. Nitin Nohria: Preparing for a Career in the Age of AI
Barry Ritholtz in conversation with Nitin Nohria, former dean of Harvard Business School and author of The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. Bloomberg Radio.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the age of artificial intelligence, how should students prepare for this job market? Let’s bring in Harvard Professor Nitin Nohria. He’s former dean of the Harvard Business School. His new book is The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility. He’s also executive chairman at Thrive Capital, which is the venture firm run by Joshua Kushner. So let’s start with AI. If artificial intelligence is attacking that entry rung of the career ladder, how should recent college grads build the skills and judgment that used to come from those entry-level jobs?

NITIN NOHRIA: First, students should continue to use their time during their education to be even more determined to cultivate critical thinking — the capacity to interrogate themselves. When I teach cases now, one thing I’ve started to do is to ask students, “Tell me what AI said about this case.” Actually, not just tell me — read to me what your AI agent said to you about this case. Because I want them to know you can use these tools. In fact, you’ll be required to use these tools when you get to work.

NITIN NOHRIA: And then I ask them the second question: What did you agree with? What did you disagree with? What further questions did you ask to get your thinking to be improved? I think this form of critical reasoning — where we rely upon AI to inform ourselves, but then we interrogate it deeply, and we learn how to think alongside it — this is a capability that they will be required to have, and I think the best students will prepare themselves this way.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So your preference is, rather than just become a very inch-wide, mile-deep domain expert, really have the broad meta-skills — critical reading, critical thinking, and a more intelligent form of learning and working with AI. Is that the takeaway?

NITIN NOHRIA: I think so. My view increasingly is that you should think of AI very much like in the Marvel comics. Each person can develop their own superpower. You don’t need a Marvel suit; AI becomes the equivalent of your Marvel suit. But you have to tune it to yourself, right? It’s not like all Marvel heroes have the same superpowers. You will develop your own superpowers, and that’ll be your distinctive edge. How you use this extraordinary capacity to distinguish yourself, to make yourself special — that will be the new edge that people will have to find.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So, undergraduate: does the major a student takes really matter? We saw such a push towards STEM, but now it seems a lot of those technical skills are getting commoditized. How should a student be thinking about what they should be studying, how they develop judgment and communication skills? How important is the major?

NITIN NOHRIA: In the same metaphor that I used — you have to find what your unique Marvel superpower is — expertise could be one of them. It is not the case that expertise disappears. If you end up being the person who has dug deep into computer science, and you can therefore answer questions about the right way to program using AI, about the right way to create safety — all of the questions that are now being worked on by the leading researchers at the top labs — that’s not something that I, who doesn’t have that same level of intuition, experience, and expertise, will be able to do.

NITIN NOHRIA: For others, it may be writing. For others, it may be history. So I do think that a major will continue to be important. But then there will be people who take interdisciplinary majors — like Social Studies at Harvard — who say, “I’m not going to differentiate myself on expertise, because that will be for some people. I’m going to be the generalist.” And I think that being a generalist is going to be deeply important in this world too.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, no doubt. So let’s talk about that first job, which, when I was coming up, was described as the all-important first job. Is that still the case? Should people think about that first gig out of college as something that’s a little bit of an experiment, to figure out what they like and what they’re good at? Or should it be a commitment to the company, to the industry, to their bosses — just jump in with both feet? Or somewhere in between?

NITIN NOHRIA: In my experience, having taught for now almost 40 years — I teach mostly business school students, who are graduate students, but I’ve also had interaction with lots of undergraduate students — I find that students are of two types. There are people who, somewhere very early in their life, know exactly what their life’s mission is. I’ve always said to those people: get on with it. Find a place, commit, dig deep, because you already know what you want to do. Don’t waste time flitting around running experiments. The experiment of your life is already known. Now you have to find a way to deliver on it.

NITIN NOHRIA: And there are other people — and I will put myself in that category — who didn’t have a clue about what I wanted to do when I joined an undergraduate institution. Didn’t even have a clue when I went to graduate school, and had to discover through experimentation what it was that I was going to be good at. For those people, I say: don’t be afraid of experimentation. Don’t get anxious that you don’t know exactly what you want to do. But when you get the signal that this is what you want to do, listen hard. Your body, mind, and heart will tell you that this is what you were meant to do. And when that happens, lock in and pursue it with all your heart. But don’t get impatient if you don’t know very early on what it is that you want to do, and cut yourself some grace.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really interesting advice. So, you’re executive chairman of a venture capital firm. I’ve played around in that space over the years, and one of the things I’m kind of fascinated by is how often startups — really very new companies — pivot from the initial idea to a variation, to a derivative of the original technology, and sometimes to something entirely different. How should students and new grads think about those career pivots? How should they think about, “Hey, is this just tough and I have to fight my way through? Or am I really more interested in this adjacent area of practice?”

NITIN NOHRIA: For entrepreneurs, there’s a level of persistence and a willingness to pivot as needed, because there’s such a determination to come up with the right solution for a problem that may initially have presented as A, but over time looks like it’s its adjacency. A colleague of mine, Amar Bhidé, did research at Harvard Business School on hundreds of entrepreneurs, and he found that in 80% of the cases, as you said, where they ended up was a distant cousin at best of what they started with — even when they were successful. And I think that’s not very different from people who pursue careers.

NITIN NOHRIA: Even if you’re not an entrepreneur, where you start may not be where you end up in your career. You may start as a consultant because that feels like the right way to gain some experience. You may start as a journalist, and you could end up in very different places. So I think people should remain permanently open to exploring adjacencies that they’re drawn to — and certainly to recognizing when what they’re doing is a dead end and it’s not going to actually yield anything. It’s the hardest thing for people to do sometimes, to recognize a dead end. But I also say to people: don’t be too quick to allow irritations or frictions to be seen as a dead end.

NITIN NOHRIA: So I say to people, if you’re unhappy, allow yourself to be unhappy for at least three to six months before you decide that this is a dead end. Because if you switch every time you experience unhappiness, you’re just never going to have the persistence to work through the things that you have to work through in almost any job or any career.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: That persistence reminds me of a quote I’ve heard about so many different areas, and I want to see how much it applies to a career: it should be treated as a marathon, not a sprint. True?
NITIN NOHRIA: One hundred percent. And yet, as you know, a marathon is not run at the same pace.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Sure.

NITIN NOHRIA: If you see the great runners in a marathon, they try and set the pace early. So sometimes you want to actually set the pace early. In the middle of the race you might slow down, but you’re always trying to set a pace. At times you want to run with the group; at times you want to run alone. So yes, a marathon is a long race, but it’s not run at the same cadence throughout. I think that’s what a good career looks like as well.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Tell us about experiential learning. How should universities and students design higher education so that students really get the most out of their four years or so in college, and are best prepared for a career?

NITIN NOHRIA: I’m a huge proponent of experiential learning — but, full disclosure, I’m very biased in this regard. I think the case method that we taught by at Harvard Business School was an opportunity for students to confront experience in the classroom. In many ways, I used to think of it as the best flight simulation that you could have in business. We can’t possibly put you into a hundred business situations in the real world, but we can give you 90 minutes of simulation of different business problems. And in each case, you have to act as the protagonist. You have to think about the problem with no solution given.

NITIN NOHRIA: So that’s one form of experiential learning. But then, in my time as dean, we asked every one of our students to travel abroad, to get involved in real company situations. I think the only way to test whether the ideas that you’re learning play out in practice — how you apply your judgment — is through experiential learning. And I believe that in an age of AI, where the knowledge you have available will be at your fingertips, learning how to apply it in practical, experiential contexts will be the one profoundly powerful way of cultivating the kind of critical thinking and judgment I started our conversation with.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: You know, I was speaking with Bob Michele — he’s the head of fixed income at J.P. Morgan — and he has this quote that he tells his interns: the way to differentiate yourself is mastering AI tools the way my generation had to master the spreadsheet. Good advice?
NITIN NOHRIA: Very good advice.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Alright, our last two questions — and because you were dean at the Harvard Business School, these are going to be a little tailored to that. What is the prestige trap? What is the issue with chasing brand-name employers? Is that a sound strategy?

NITIN NOHRIA: Brands are brands because they reflect something real. I don’t think brands can sustain themselves if they don’t reflect real opportunities. So if you go to Goldman Sachs, there is something that you will learn at Goldman Sachs that’s important. Or if you go to JPMorgan Chase in banking. If you go to consulting firms like BCG, Bain & Company, McKinsey — these are brands that carry cachet because they’re important. If you are interested in media, you go to Bloomberg or Disney. These are good places to go because the brands carry something.

NITIN NOHRIA: But I think increasingly, I find at Harvard Business School that many of our students have learned that there’s a lot to be learned in places that are not brands. So the courage that people now have to start in places that aren’t already established brands has dramatically increased. And the reason that increases, I think, is that these people have come of age where great companies have been built in front of their eyes. Who knew what Facebook was going to be? Who knew what Google was going to be? In the span of 10, 15 years, extraordinary brands have been built. And so I think our students have become much more comfortable saying that while a brand provides some assurance of a good learning experience, I can also get a great learning experience if I put myself in a setting where there’s a lot more risk — but if it succeeds, it can succeed in an extraordinary way.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: And the question I’m very curious about: you’ve not only taught decades of students at Harvard, at the business school and elsewhere as well. I’m curious — what career paths of alumni from the Harvard Business School really surprised you?

NITIN NOHRIA: I think the thing that has constantly surprised me is when our students decide to stake out their own entrepreneurial journey. Fifty percent of our business school students, by the end of their careers, will have chosen an entrepreneurial path. And it can be anything from opening their own small consulting firm, to at some point deciding to start their own investment shop, to buying a small company, or even sometimes returning to their family company and deciding, “I want to run this company.”

NITIN NOHRIA: So it’s interesting. In the end, people want to have the opportunity to feel like, “I am reporting to no boss. I have ownership over what I’m building.” And yet some people will do it as soon as they graduate from the school; some people will do it 25 years later. What has constantly surprised me is: what’s the trigger that finally causes someone to say, “Okay, I now need to have the opportunity to be an entrepreneur”? And it’s amazing the different ways in which people arrive at that decision.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really fascinating stuff. Thank you for being so generous with your time, Professor Nohria. We have been speaking with Nitin Nohria, author of the new book The CEO: The Role, the Reality, and the Responsibility, and former dean of the Harvard Business School. You’ve been listening to Bloomberg’s At The Money.

6a4dc94a574c50d8: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.”
In a follow-up message, Yen reiterated his point: “only losers think like that.” His ultimate message for the team was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. Proton is a Swiss company that famously makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, a password manager, and more.

In the last few months, Yen set up an email address for employees to contact if they come across anything blocking adoption of AI at Proton, so leadership can “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity;” Proton installed software on workers’ computers that track how much AI code the company is generating; and Yen said this is the last year that Proton will hire engineers at all, and instead only hire people to build things with AI.

That AI push came to head this week when 404 Media reported Proton said it would re-interview staff about their use of AI, with the clear implication that those interviews, and employees’ willingness to embrace AI, could decide whether a worker is fired or not.

404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.
“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” one of the sources told 404 Media.

Our reporting also paints a picture of Proton that is likely very different to the public’s perception of a company with a goal of carefully protecting privacy: one that in reality is barreling ahead with AI as quickly as possible so it can achieve the explicit goal of more annual revenue.

“Due to insufficient velocity,” Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year, one internal document obtained by 404 Media reads. Proton’s year-over-year growth is also “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”
In response to detailed questions from 404 Media, a Proton spokesperson did not dispute any of our reporting or characterization of what’s happening inside of the company.

“It’s clear that some people at Proton are unhappy with our direction, or misunderstand it, and many people are anxious,” they said. “In our determination to move fast, we have sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining ourselves to our people. We will work on that, as their questions are the ones we most need to answer.”
Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.
10696ec422baa2f8: The Hora 1 site is at the base of this peak of rock in northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NDIn the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next? We know that ancient people lived by foraging their food from wild plants and animals, but we know a lot less about their social lives. Would there be conflict as people defended territory? Or would they choose to share? Sometimes survival depends on choosing wisely between these options. Defending a territory has a cost, and it’s not always worth it. To understand how ancient people interacted with one another, we can start by looking at the food they ate. When food resources are densely clustered in predictable ways, it makes sense to establish and maintain a territory around them. When resources are sparsely distributed, they are harder to defend. One example of territoriality in modern foraging people comes from the Okiek in the mountains of Kenya. Here, families control the crucially important activity of honey-harvesting. In contrast, foraging groups that live in places where the next meal is less predictable also tend to be less territorial. For example, until recently !Kung foragers in the arid parts of the Kalahari Desert searched for animals to hunt across wide areas, and boundaries between groups were much more fluid. A smoky torch used to harvest honey. Jessica Thompson, CC BY-ND The strategies used by the Okiek and the !Kung are different solutions to the same problem: weighing the risk of going hungry against the risk of unfriendly social encounters. Applying this principle to archaeological finds can reveal clues about ancient human social organisation. The problem is how to find food remains from the ancient past. We are archaeologists who do research in Malawi, excavating fossil animal bones and stone tools from natural shelters of rock. Our aim is to understand how early humans lived from the end of the last ice age, between 19,000 and 10,000 years ago, until the start of farming and herd-keeping just a few thousand years ago. Although no glaciers were present in tropical Malawi during the last ice age, global environments were different from today. We wanted to know more about food availability then, and how this might have affected social interactions. We focused on a large shelter called Hora 1, located on a spectacular granite mountain that emerges like a tooth from the open woodlands in northern Malawi. Traces of ancient human activity are everywhere in this area: red coloured paintings on the rock walls, stone tools made of shiny quartz, hearths, human burials and, in the layers of earth carefully excavated over several visits, hundreds of thousands of bones. These are the remnants of uncountable meals for the communities who lived here. Hora Mountain rising from the landscape of northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NC Of this formidable number of broken, cooked, cut, chewed and discarded animal parts we were able to identify almost 13,000 individual fragments, collectively spanning the last 21,000 years of human occupation. We have published a paper about these fragments and what they tell us about ancient cultural boundaries related to food availability. Our findings challenge the existing view that it was mostly coastal environments that promoted boundary formation in the past. Hunting close to home Large animals can provide a meal for a large group, so when hunters encounter them, they may prefer to chase them, even if that means ignoring smaller prey. But most of the bones we found belonged to small animals: tiny antelopes, hares, monkeys, and other creatures. That suggests that large prey with a lot of meat – like zebras, wildebeest and even rhinoceroses – were not very common in this valley in the past. Although the fragments were very small, we could see that they came from everywhere in the body: limbs, torsos and heads were all present. This suggests that these animals were hunted close to the site, and the whole carcass was brought back (not just the best parts of large animals). The bones indicate that foragers at Hora 1 hunted close to home throughout the thousands of years recorded in the archaeological deposits. We confirmed this by comparing the chemistry of the local geology to chemical traces in the animal teeth: we found that they matched. The fossil tooth of a wildebeest from HOR-1, an animal that has not been recorded in modern times in this part of Malawi. The lines in the tooth are where small samples were taken for chemical analysis. Ruoyang Tu, CC BY-NC But there is a twist to this story. The animal bones were extremely fragmented, on average only the size of a little finger. Then we looked at some of the smallest and most nutrient poor bones in the skeleton: the phalanges, or finger and toe bones. Most had been broken open to recover even the smallest amounts of fatty marrow from inside. Probably food was not so abundant in this valley if people spent their time on such meagre packages of nutrients. So why didn’t people just range further to find more food, and what kept them at that site for so long? We think the answer lies in their social worlds. In-group cooperation and out-group hostility We found that animals were of different ages when they died: youngsters, adults, and even animals so old their teeth were worn down. This suggests some form of indiscriminate mass hunting such as the use of nets or traps. It is also possible that fire was used to aid communal game drives of larger animals. All these practices would have required coordination of labour, as well as social norms on how to split the bounty. This in-group cooperation likely came with some sense of shared identity, like a cultural group. The next question is how far across the landscape this group would have roamed. Were they like the !Kung, who maintain strong social ties with neighbouring groups? Or were they more like the Okiek, focused on keeping resources within their families? A clue came from an unexpected source: ancient DNA. DNA preserved in some of the human burials found at these sites showed that relatedness became smaller very quickly as one moved further from the sites. Starting 19,000 years ago, at the end of the ice age, an invisible boundary was taking shape in tropical Africa, separating “us and them”. Ancient human DNA was recovered from ancient foragers buried at Hora 1 and at this cave, which is about 100km north of the Hora 1 site. Jacob Davis, CC BY-NC All this evidence together points to behaviour that was very “local” in nature. However, the focus on recovering every scrap of food suggests that prey were not abundant enough to justify active defence of this territory. We also do not see evidence for persistent violent encounters or large, stable settlements, as have been documented near rich sources of food such as lakes and oceans. It is possible that these boundaries were only symbolically defended, for instance through collective practices like the 9,500-year-old funerary pyre that we recently described from Hora 1. Read more: Oldest known cremation in Africa poses 9,500-year-old mystery about Stone Age hunter-gatherers Most “cultural groups” that are known from archaeology are inferred from durable artifacts that preserve well, such as ornaments made of animal teeth and shells, or pottery shaped in a specific way. But most foragers spent so much time on the move that they never made such heavy things. In tropical Africa, our research has unearthed evidence for ancient cultural boundaries even without these objects. We have also found that there can be a “home” territory and a strong sense of in-group cultural belonging without violence against other groups. Finally, we have shown that the vast interior of the continent, while less studied than its coasts, is a rich source of information on the evolution of human cooperation and competition. Alex Bertacchi received funding for this research from the US National Science Foundation. Jessica C. Thompson has received funding for excavations at the Hora 1 site from the National Geographic Society, Wenner-Gren Foundation, Emory University, and Yale University.
e6f6442f7057ac5e: When people view sexualised images of women, they tend to remember them less well than sexualised images of men; a quirk of memory that psychologists link to objectification. But in our new study, my colleagues and I found an unlikely “fix” – applying a mild electrical current to the forehead. Objectification means seeing someone as a body, or a set of body parts, rather than as a whole person. Our results, published in Social Neuroscience, suggest this bias in perception is not hard-wired and can be changed – at least for a while. Psychologists measure it with an upside-down test. People are much better at recognising faces and bodies the right way up – typically about 80% right, against 55% upside down – because we take in how all the parts fit together. With objects, such as houses, turning them over matters far less, because we recognise them by their parts. A 2012 study used this test on sexualised images. Volunteers briefly saw a photo, then had to pick it out from a pair: the photo itself and its mirror image. Men and women alike did far better with men in underwear when the photos were upright, but did about as well with women in similar poses either way – the pattern expected for objects. The finding has been debated, and some attempts to repeat it have failed. But a 2022 analysis pooling results from 41 papers found the “upright advantage” – how much better people recognise someone the right way up than upside down – is smaller for sexualised women than sexualised men. Sexually objectified women are seen as less competent and less fully human, and women who absorb this view of themselves tend to have poorer body image and worse mental, physical and sexual health. Exposure to sexualised media is also linked to greater tolerance of sexual violence against women. The bias also shifts with circumstances. In a 2015 study, blurring out women’s chests and groins, or describing them as medical graduates raising money for cancer research, made people recognise their bodies more like men’s. Power plays a part. In earlier research in Canada, a colleague and I asked people to spend ten minutes writing about a time they had power over someone, or when someone had power over them. An established way to make people feel powerful or powerless. Women who felt powerful showed the object-like pattern for sexualised men, and powerful men showed it for sexualised women. People who felt powerless showed the upright advantage for both. Power, rather than gender itself, may be central to objectification. Where the brain stimulation idea came from The idea of trying brain stimulation came from my lab’s work on a famous illusion. In the Thatcher illusion, first shown with a photo of the former British prime minister, a face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks grotesque the right way up but almost normal upside down. Turning “Thatcherised” faces upside down also hurts recognition much less than it does with ordinary faces – just as with sexualised women. We had found that the same weak current made Thatcherised faces easier to recognise the right way up, bringing back the usual difference. Would it do the same for sexualised women? The Thatcher illusion. In our new study, 76 university students tried to memorise photos of male and female models posing in underwear – half of them upside down. They then saw the same photos again, each the same way up as before and mixed with 32 new ones, and said whether they had seen each one before. Half the students received a weak current for ten minutes, using a technique called transcranial direct current stimulation. The others received a placebo that switched off after 30 seconds – a standard way of mimicking the tingle of the real thing. Neither the students nor the researchers testing them knew who got which. The placebo group showed the familiar pattern. They remembered men far better when the photos were upright than when upside down. For women, the difference was much smaller, mainly because they remembered upright women less well than upright men. In the stimulated group, recognition of upright images of women improved, and the gap between images of men and women disappeared. The current did not change the upright advantage for images of men. Why? Our best explanation comes from a theory of how people learn to see. With experience, the brain learns to play down features that all faces share and to pick out the details that tell one person from another. But some shared features grab attention instead, such as the flipped eyes and mouth of a Thatcherised face – or, we suspect, the body parts on display in sexualised images. They crowd out the details that tell one person from another. The current may weaken that pull. Our study was a single lab session with university students, and we only measured its immediate effects, not attitudes or behaviour. Because every image was sexualised, we also cannot say how much of the gap comes from sexualisation itself rather than other differences between the photos. Brain stimulation is no cure for sexism. But if ten minutes of a weak current – or ten minutes spent writing about feeling powerful or powerless – can shift how people see a body, objectification looks less like a fixed feature of human vision and more like a habit. And habits, unlike hard-wiring, can change. Ciro Civile receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and previously from the European Union Horizon

05e64d90fcbc7502: Their petition to the authorities has already gathered over 500 signatures
Originally published on Global Voices
DigiAction picnic held in Lozhan village, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In rural parts of Albania, youth are seldom mobilized to help solve local environmental and other problems in their communities, although they, too, are affected by them. This has been the case in the eastern Korce region as well, which was hit by heavy rainfall and subsequent devastating floods in November 2025.

In the Maliq municipality, one of the affected areas, the situation was worsened by improper disposal of waste that blocked drainage channels, including the Devoll River, which flows through the area. Illegal waste disposal has obstructed the river’s infrastructure and contributed to widespread flooding. Despite efforts by the authorities to improve waste management and clean up the river, the situation has remained dire.
Waste accumulated at the Devoll River Bridge in Maliq, Albania. Photo from November 21, 2025 by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Qendra KAZUS, recruited and trained local youth to help solve this long-standing issue by turning them into environmental advocates. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Dhorjela Cela, the group’s executive director, to learn about how Qendra KAZUS implemented a project that brought together youth, digital democracy, environmental challenges, and advocacy. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Dhorjela Cule (DC): Qendra KAZUS was founded in 2024 and focuses on young people’s activism and engagement. Our team brings together journalists, photojournalists, and education specialists with years of experience in media, law, and mentoring.

Our mission is to strengthen democracy and the rule of law through youth advocacy and to raise awareness around preserving cultural heritage, protecting the environment, and building capacity in ICT and media. As a young organization, our work relied mainly on small activities and projects.

Digital Sparks gave us the opportunity to prioritize digital advocacy. We saw a chance to give young people in rural areas and cities tools they use every day — their phones and social media — and turn them into instruments of civic participation and accountability.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

DC: The Devoll River in the eastern Korça region is facing a serious environmental situation. Plastic pollution, inert waste, agricultural waste, and other debris accumulate along the riverbanks. During winter floods, high river flows expose and spread this waste, blocking drainage canals, and water overflows from the riverbed into agricultural land and residential areas, damaging soil health, livelihoods, and the local ecosystem.
In the villages of Lozhan and Pojan, the waste is considerable, and local authorities seem to have their hands tied in finding a solution.

What worried us most was that young people from rural areas, whose families depend on agriculture and are directly affected, were excluded from the search for solutions. They had phones and strong opinions, but no channel to turn them into public pressure.
We wanted to show that the right to a clean environment is something young people can demand with evidence and a collective voice.
Waste on the banks of the Devoll River in Pojan from May 2026. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

DC: We implemented three phases of the project. First, we recruited and trained 44 young people from Maliq municipality in MoJo, aiming to turn mobile storytelling, video editing for reels, and graphic design in Canva into a powerful advocacy tool.

Second, we organized two Digital Picnics along the Devoll River and the affected farmland, piloting two locations in the villages of Pojan and Lozhan, where participants filmed and photographed the accumulation of waste, creating a “visual pollution map”. Thirty materials produced by the young people were published on social media to raise public awareness.

Finally, we launched an online petition, through which we will ask the Maliq municipality to step up cleaning actions, with the joint commitment of the municipality and the community, as well as community education and awareness.
The petition was hosted on Change.org to reach a wider audience and has collected 506 signatures so far, exceeding our target.
Participants of the DigiAction Picnic in Pojan, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

DC: For the young participants, the project turned social media from an entertainment tool into a tool for action. Forty-four young people learned to document environmental problems and communicate them publicly.

“I had never seen the use of social media from this perspective. Now, I have a different approach to the posts I can make,” said Igli, one of the young people who joined the training and field activity.

For the community, the Digital Picnics made the pollution visible: everyone had the chance to see the waste accumulated along the river in videos and posts, and hundreds of people engaged with our content online.

The petition gave residents and supporters a simple way to take a stand, and 506 people signed it online. The materials now form a public archive of evidence that the community can use in future discussions with local authorities.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
DC: Through Digital Sparks, we came to understand digital democracy more broadly: using technology to document facts, mobilize people, and demand accountability from institutions.
We learned how evidence, whether a video, a poster, or a signature, gives citizens credibility when they address public authorities.

We also gained practical experience in campaign planning, content strategy, moderating online comments, using Instagram and TikTok analytics, and digital safety and ethics, including the protection of young participants and personal data.
As a team, this project taught us how to turn this knowledge into youth-led digital civic action.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

DC: One of the most valuable lessons is that in the digital era, young people need little technical equipment, but much more mentoring and guidance to lead them towards becoming responsible citizens who make demands and engage in concrete action to be part of decision-making. Their phones and creativity are enough when they have a clear purpose and guidance.
Second, an informal and enjoyable format like the Digital Picnic lowers barriers to participation and attracts young people, including girls and those from marginalized groups or low-income families.

Images and facts are more persuasive to institutions than complaints, but this experience taught us that flexibility is essential. Choosing Change.org instead of Google Forms for the petition taught us to adapt tools to the audience.
Finally, institutional change and engagement take time, and follow-up is as important as mobilization.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

DC: Qendra KAZUS has started implementing another project in which part of the knowledge gained is being applied. The use of social media by young people as a powerful mechanism to raise their voice and demand more engagement and responsibility from institutions is this time focused on cultural heritage.

What remains essential for us is identifying a completely different approach to young people, through the channels and platforms where they spend a considerable part of their time and focus their communication.

It is worth stressing that finding a meeting point with young people, through a method that is interesting to them, is of particular importance. We have managed to involve them by showing that social media can also be used as a healthy mechanism that achieves results for their demands.
Written by Nurbek Bekmurzaev
95da20d12b9a0c2b: Like the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal is a vital waterway for global trade. Viktor Hladchenko/ShutterstockMonths after the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. The UK chose not to get directly involved in the conflict. Nonetheless, it has been exposed to the crisis through record-high diesel prices as well as a spike in inflation. This echoes an earlier crisis in the Middle East, as my recent research illustrates. Seventy years ago, the Egyptian government nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the Suez crisis. The canal, which passes through Egypt from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, was a vital link for ships travelling between Europe and Asia. After its completion in 1869 by a French-led company, the Egyptian government held a 44% stake in it. However, financial difficulties forced Egypt to sell its shares to the British government in 1875, leaving Britain and France with substantial financial interests in the canal. Following the Egyptian nationalisation of the canal, France and Britain – together with Israel – invaded Egypt in an attempt to regain control of the vital waterway. But the invasion was a spectacular failure that was condemned by the international community. The crisis came to symbolise Britain’s loss of superpower status. Today, the US midterm elections are increasing the pressure on the Trump administration over the current conflict. Elections in Israel have also had some bearing on the conflict, with recent reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for renewed strikes ahead of the election. Other reports suggest that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to resume strikes after the elections. In 1956, US presidential elections were also an important part of the calculus. But back then, Britain and France had assumed that the elections would distract the US from their actions. This was a miscalculation. In communication with UK Prime Minister Anthony Eden the day after the vote, US President Dwight D. Eisenhower was clear that his administration would not tolerate the UK, France and Israel’s continued actions. He demanded a negotiated settlement through the UN. The parallels between Suez and Hormuz go beyond the closure of two vital waterways. Both crises raise the same question: how far can geopolitical power outrun economic power? Superpowers in decline In 1944, the American foreign policy professor William T.R. Fox coined the term “super-power”. He defined it as the consequence of “great wealth, great population, and favourable geographic position”. This is similar to how the historian Phillips O’Brien defines great power today. Fox saw three superpowers at that time: the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union. He later acknowledged that including Britain had been a mistake, primarily because of its relative decline against the US and later the rest of Europe. Arguably a similar shift is taking place today. There are arguments over what is the best measure of an economy, but on the basis of purchasing power the shift is striking. China has moved from being a fraction of the size of the US economy in 1990 to being well ahead today. In the 19th century, Britain was the dominant global power and benefited from what economists call “exorbitant privilege”. This was the ability to easily finance debt at favourable interest rates because sterling played a central role in the international monetary system. London was also the world’s leading financial centre. But as Britain declined, this privilege gradually shifted towards the US. Its loss became particularly pressing during the Suez crisis as the pound came under intense pressure. Similarly today, there are signs of strain in the financial system that underpins American power. During the Suez crisis, Britain’s currency weakness and dependence on American financial support constrained its ability to act independently, despite its considerable military power. The crisis was also part of wider cold war geopolitics. An arms deal signed in 1955 between Egypt and the Soviet Union had upset the regional balance of power and contributed to Israel’s decision to get involved in a preventative war. In response to the arms deal, the US withdrew financing for the Aswan Dam, a major infrastructure project on the River Nile. Then, in 1956, Egypt nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the crisis. British leaders sought to portray Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser as a 1930s dictator, intent on regional dominance. Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956. Wikimedia Commons The US intervention in Iran has similar connotations. US secretary of war Pete Hegseth has presented the assassination of the Iranian leadership as necessary to prevent an existential threat from “America’s mortal enemy”. Geoeconomics, the relationship between economics and geopolitics, also played a central role in the Suez crisis. The canal was a major conduit for Middle Eastern oil and there were fears that the nationalisation of the canal would disrupt UK oil supplies. But ironically, it was the decision to invade Egypt that led to a shortage of oil and fuel rationing in the UK. The wider cold war was a key factor in the US stance on events. The US did not want to be seen to be condoning imperial actions in Egypt while condemning Russian imperialism in Hungary. Just as the Suez crisis needs to be understood in the context of the cold war, the current conflict should also be seen through the lens of “cold war II” geopolitics. Relations between the US and China have not thawed, while proxy wars bear similarities to the first cold war. Today, the US is increasingly stretched, most clearly seen in the depletion of its munitions. These were already under pressure (in part because of its support for Ukraine) and have been further reduced by the war with Iran. The Suez crisis illustrates how political leaders can be slow to appreciate the economic constraints on their geopolitical ambitions. The US today is not Britain in 1956, yet the conflict in Iran has prompted questions about the limits of American power. As its relative economic dominance is challenged, will the US also have to reconsider the extent of its global military commitments? e5d6004b39bc62dd: Some local papers that were on the verge of extinction, like the Solon Economist in Iowa, have teamed up with universities as a way to get staffing and support. Photo from Teri Finneman, CC BYCatherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024. But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa. It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets. These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston. We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis. Knowing your community These experiments come against a grim backdrop. Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years. But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists. How the University of Iowa stepped in to save the Solon Economist. Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work. Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently. In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers. The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff. “They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.” Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines. Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships. Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.” “People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.” Chris Umscheid, editor of the Solon Economist, says the paper’s mission remains serving the community by reporting local news, but now with more staff. Teri Finneman, CC BY The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger. Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000. Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.” A $10 deal Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo. Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up. How the Oglethorpe Echo found a new owner. “I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.” NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership. In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added. The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed. Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county. The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds. She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit. When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester. Amanda Bright’s journalism students at The University of Georgia rotate across different roles to develop writing, editing and multimedia skills. Teri Finneman, CC BY The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said. But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat. But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said. Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added. Service over profits One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships. The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances. These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting. Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view. “Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.” Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U." Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
2bdab1e31b4111b6: An 1805 European map depicting the mythical Mountains of Kong range. Wikimedia CommonsAfter the United Nations adopted a resolution in September 2026 endorsing a map that more fairly represents the size of Earth’s landmasses, author and journalist Moky Makura of Africa No Filter – a main sponsor of the Correct the Map initiative – asked: “What else about Africa is the world underestimating that’s also hidden in plain sight?” It is a fair question. The initiative brought attention to the way continents are distorted by projections that display our rotund planet on two-dimensional maps, something that has long made Africa especially appear far smaller than it actually is. But it left another assumption untouched: that European maps of Africa – which became the basis of how we see African countries today – are based solely on the observations of the Europeans who made them. As an expert on the map history of Africa, I know that this is a misconception which deserves rethinking. Recent research by myself and others on colonial-era mapping of West Africa demonstrates that much of the geographical information these maps show is based on African observations. It’s just that Europeans largely took the credit. A line in the sand Most African map traditions are undocumented or ephemeral. But ground and oral mapping was common in the pre-colonial period, and often highly valued. European explorers relied upon these indigenous mapping practices during their travels and sometimes incorporated them into their own maps. For example, sections of French explorer Henri Duveyrier’s 1861 map of the Sahara owed much to the maps drawn in the sand by his guide, Cheikh‐‘Othmàn. Indeed, more than a third of Duveyrier’s map is based on information provided by local sources. Part of Henri Duveyrier’s and Edouard de Desbuisson’s 1861 map of the western Sahara showing African-sourced routes in solid black lines and European-surveyed routes in solid red lines. Bibliothèque nationale de France A common objective of mapping is to solve a spatial problem. Route mapping is all about finding one’s way between points A and B and determining the distances between them. For Europeans, it was important to know where African leaders resided or the most direct route to important trade centers. When European explorers and soldier-surveyors inquired, African guides, interpreters and merchants described the road ahead and often drew these routes on the ground with a stick. Europeans valued African oral and ground-mapping practices for their contributions to knowledge; they were also useful for empire building. In his 1892 travel memoir, French Navy Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger reproduced the plan of Niellé, a city in contemporary northern Ivory Coast that was drawn on the ground by his interpreter, Fofana Diawé. African guides and interpreters, Fofana Diawé and Moussa Diawara, contributed to Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger’s 1887-1889 exploration and mapping of the Niger River Bend region of West Africa. Binger/Du Niger au Golfe de Guinée par le pays de Kong et le Mossi Niellé’s chief prohibited Binger from visiting the town, making Diawé’s drawing particularly valuable. In another instance, Binger reports that an African intermediary placed varied lengths of straw on the ground to indicate the distances between localities in the Kong region. In his exploration of the area between the Niger River and the Gulf of Guinea in the early 1890s, Navy Lt. Jean-Baptiste Marchand routinely collected route information from local inhabitants about places he could not visit. This “locally sourced route information,” as he described it, appears as dashed lines on his landmark map of the region. The routes of Marchand and other European explorers appear as solid lines. African guide and interpreter Fofana Diawé’s ground map of Niellé reproduced by French Navy Lt. Louis-Gustave Binger. Binger, 1882 When the total distance of all routes is calculated, African sources account for 65% of routes on Marchand’s map. Thanks to African intermediaries guiding these military explorers, Binger discovered that the fabled Kong Mountains, which stretched across most 19th-century maps, did not exist. And Marchand learned that the savanna penetrated more deeply into the rainforest in south-central Ivory Coast. The elimination of the imaginary Kong Mountains and knowledge of a shorter travel distance through the dense tropical forest accelerated French colonization of the region. But this practice of displaying locally sourced route information on European maps was debated among European geographers and military officers. Some mapmakers refused to display African mapping because it did not follow the standards of scientific cartography. They argued that the geographical information was based on hearsay rather than measurement. Others, particularly military officers trying to expand colonial boundaries, appreciated locally made maps’ practical value. Embedded in this debate was the self-claimed civilizing mission ideology underpinning colonialism, which assumed the superiority of European knowledge. The dashed lines suggest that locally sourced information was tentative and would eventually be replaced by solid lines based on European measurements. A digitized version of Jean-Baptiste Marchand’s 1896 map of part of West Africa. Locally sourced route information is shown in blue dashed lines. Afriterra – The Cartographic Free Library. Filling in the blanks The appearance of blank spaces on maps is typically seen as demonstrating the scientific standard of accuracy: Cartographers don’t show what we don’t know. Blank spaces were also viewed as instrumental to imperial expansion. That’s because they suggested vacant areas open to colonization. The common denominator of both views is that Europeans determine what is shown and not shown on maps of Africa. But a closer look at explorers’ and soldier-surveyors’ reports indicates that blank spaces often emerged from the refusal of African authorities to allow Europeans to travel through their territory. Wisely, these African rulers understood the ultimate goals of European soldier-surveyors – to map the road to colonial conquest. In the memoir of his exploration of contemporary Mali, Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso, Binger explained the blank spaces on his four-sheet map as deriving from his lack of “a good guide and a travel permit [from African authorities].” To try to overcome this lack of access, colonial officials employed Africans to explore and map. Traces of their little-known expeditions appear in late 19th- and early 20th-century compilation maps assembled by European mapmakers. The travel routes of two Senegalese explorers, Roger Panet in 1850 and Bou El Mogdad Seck around a decade later, appear in Hermann Habenicht’s ten-sheet map of Africa published in 1885-1886. Bou El-Mogdad, Senegalese interpreter and explorer, who mapped a route from northern Senegal to west-central Morocco in 1860-1861. Le Tour du Monde,/Wikimedia Commons The central Africa mapping of two Africans working as Portuguese trade agents, Pedro Joao Baptista and Amaro José, is depicted on the “Kabébé” sheet of Régnauld de Lannoy de Bissy’s 63-sheet map of Africa. The display of their itineraries in solid lines alongside those of Europeans indicates their equal treatment by Lannoy. Lannoy also used the dashed-line symbol to show locally sourced geographical information. More than two-thirds of the route information displayed in his 1882 Segou-Sikoro sheet stems from African mapping practices. Both maps were used at the Berlin Africa Conference of 1884-85 to determine the boundaries of free trade zones in the Congo and Niger river basins. The conference kick-started the “scramble for Africa” that was to last into the 20th century. Paradoxically, the maps that Africans helped construct were later used to divide their territories into European colonies. Decades after decolonization, when we open the drawers of national archives, we find these remarkable maps with their solid and dashed lines. And map historians are finally acknowledging that these maps, cataloged as purely European achievements, are in fact hybrid productions that emerged from complex intercultural encounters. The evidence was hidden in plain sight.
